card.headline: Alert rabbit with bright, clean eyes
card.look: A healthy rabbit sits up alert, ears responsive to sounds, with clear eyes, a dry clean nose and a smooth, shiny coat. It nibbles hay or greens through much of the day and leaves plenty of round, dry droppings.
card.action: Look at every rabbit, its feed and its droppings every morning and evening, and call the vet the same day if one stops eating or stops passing droppings.

detail.summary: This page describes what a normal, healthy rabbit looks, sounds and behaves like, so you can spot problems early. Rabbits are prey animals and naturally hide pain and illness, so changes are often small at first. By the time a rabbit looks obviously sick it may be seriously ill. Knowing the healthy baseline for your own rabbits is the most useful health tool any rabbit farmer can have.
detail.cause: A rabbit stays healthy when its gut, teeth, housing and stress levels are all in balance. The rabbit's digestive system is built to process large amounts of fibre, mainly from hay and grasses. Fibre keeps the gut moving, feeds the helpful bacteria in the caecum (a large pouch at the start of the large intestine where food is fermented) and wears down the teeth. A rabbit's teeth grow throughout its life, so constant chewing of rough fibre keeps them the right length. The caecum produces soft, sticky droppings called caecotrophs, which the rabbit eats straight from its bottom, usually at night or early morning, to take in vitamins and protein made by gut bacteria. This is completely normal and essential. Rabbits cannot vomit, so anything that slows the gut, such as low fibre, too much starch or sugar, sudden feed changes, stress or pain, can quickly lead to a dangerous gut slowdown. Clean, dry, well-ventilated housing protects the lungs from ammonia (the sharp smell from urine) and reduces coccidia and other germs. Shade and airflow matter because rabbits do not sweat and cope poorly with heat. Calm handling, enough space and a steady routine keep stress low, which keeps the immune system strong.
spread: Good health builds from a high-fibre diet: unlimited clean hay or dry grass forms the base, with fresh greens and a measured amount of rabbit pellets on top.
Clean, fresh drinking water available at all times keeps digestion moving and helps the rabbit cope with heat, even when it eats plenty of greens.
Gradual feed changes over about one to two weeks give gut bacteria time to adjust; sudden changes are a common trigger for bloat and diarrhoea.
Dry, clean hutches with regular removal of droppings and wet bedding reduce coccidiosis, sore hocks and breathing problems.
Good ventilation without strong draughts keeps ammonia low and protects the nose and lungs.
Shade and cool housing during hot months and in hot lowland areas prevent heat stress.
Quarantining new rabbits for about two to three weeks before they join the herd keeps mange, snuffles and other infections out.
Calm, correct handling, supporting the back and hindquarters, prevents injuries and reduces fear and stress.
detail.atRisk: Every rabbit benefits from regular health checks, but some need closer watching. Young rabbits around weaning, usually four to eight weeks old, are the most fragile because their gut is still adapting and they are prone to diarrhoea and coccidiosis. Pregnant and nursing does need more water and good feed, and their condition can drop quickly. Older rabbits are more likely to develop tooth problems and arthritis. Heavy, thick-coated breeds such as Flemish Giant, and long-haired rabbits, suffer more in heat, while all breeds common in Kenya, including New Zealand White, Californian and Chinchilla, are sensitive to high temperatures. The hot, dry months and hot lowland areas raise the risk of heat stress, while the long and short rains bring damp hutches, wet or mouldy forage and more breathing and gut problems. Rabbits in crowded, poorly cleaned or poorly ventilated hutches, and those fed mostly on kitchen waste, wet greens or too many pellets with little hay, are at higher risk of illness.

early: The rabbit is alert and curious, with ears moving towards sounds, and it comes forward or reacts normally when you approach the hutch.
Eyes are bright, clear and fully open, with no discharge, crust, cloudiness or wet fur below them.
The nose is clean and dry or slightly damp, with no white or yellow discharge and no matted fur on the inside of the front legs, which rabbits use to wipe their faces.
The coat is smooth, clean and even, with no bald patches, crusts, dandruff or dirty, wet fur around the bottom.
Droppings are plentiful, round, dry, fairly uniform in size and crumble when pressed; a healthy adult produces a large number each day.
Caecotrophs, if you see them, are soft, shiny, dark clusters like a small bunch of grapes, usually eaten straight from the bottom so you rarely find them.
The rabbit eats hay or grass on and off through the day and night, drinks regularly and chews with a steady side-to-side motion.
Normal body temperature is about 38.5–40 °C, breathing is quiet and even through the nose, and the rabbit moves with a smooth hop, using all four legs.
advanced: Eating less, refusing pellets or favourite greens, or not eating at all is an urgent warning sign in a rabbit.
Small, few, misshapen or no droppings for around 12 hours or more suggests gut slowdown, which can become life-threatening quickly.
Sitting hunched in a corner, reluctant to move, eyes half-closed, or loud teeth grinding usually means pain.
Runny or sticky droppings, a dirty wet bottom, or uneaten caecotrophs piling up in the hutch point to a gut or diet problem.
Discharge from the nose or eyes, sneezing, wet fur on the front legs, or noisy or open-mouth breathing suggest infection or heat stress.
Drooling, a wet chin, dropping food, or chewing awkwardly may mean overgrown or damaged teeth.
Head tilt, losing balance, scratching ears constantly, crusty ears, bald or scabby patches, or a swollen belly all need a vet check.
Temperature below about 38 °C or above about 40.5 °C, especially with dullness, is a serious sign; lying stretched out panting with hot ears in hot weather is heat stress.

lookalikes.name: Eating caecotrophs (mistaken for a bad habit or diarrhoea)
lookalikes.howToTell: Healthy rabbits eat soft, shiny caecotrophs straight from the bottom, usually at night or early morning. This is normal. Diarrhoea is watery or pasty, smells bad, soils the fur around the bottom and comes with fewer normal round droppings.

lookalikes.name: Red, orange or cloudy urine (mistaken for blood)
lookalikes.howToTell: Plant pigments can turn normal rabbit urine yellow, orange, red or brown, and extra calcium can make it cloudy or chalky. A healthy rabbit with coloured urine still eats, drinks and behaves normally. Real blood often appears as spots or streaks, may come with straining or a wet bottom, and needs a vet.

lookalikes.name: Moulting (mistaken for mange or ringworm)
lookalikes.howToTell: During a moult, fur comes out in tufts or lines, often with a visible line of new fur, and the skin underneath looks clean and smooth. Mange and ringworm cause crusts, scabs, flaky or thickened skin and itching, often around the ears, face, nose or feet.

lookalikes.name: Nest building and fur pulling by a doe
lookalikes.howToTell: A pregnant or falsely pregnant doe carries hay in her mouth and pulls fur from her chest, belly and dewlap (the fold of skin under the chin) to line a nest, usually near kindling. She stays bright and keeps eating. Fur loss with scabs, sores or itching is a skin problem, not nesting.

detail.diagnosis: A home health check takes a few minutes and is best done at the same time each day, ideally at feeding. First, watch before touching: is the rabbit alert, eating, moving normally and breathing quietly? Check the feed and water from yesterday and count roughly how many droppings there are and what they look like. Then handle the rabbit calmly on a non-slip surface such as a sack on a table. Never lift a rabbit by its ears or the loose skin alone. Place one hand under the chest and the other under the hindquarters, and hold it close to your body. Rabbits can break their backs if they kick hard while unsupported. Look at the eyes, nose, ears, teeth (gently lift the lips to see the front teeth meet evenly), front legs, coat, belly, feet and bottom. Feel along the spine and hips: you should feel bones under a slight layer of flesh, not sharp bones and not thick fat. To take temperature, use a digital thermometer with a flexible tip, lubricated with a little petroleum jelly. It is easiest with two people: one holds the rabbit securely on its back or side, supporting the spine, while the other gently inserts only the tip, about 1–2 cm, into the rectum at a slight angle and waits for the beep. Normal is about 38.5–40 °C. Stop if the rabbit struggles hard. Breathing is normally about 30–60 breaths a minute at rest, faster when warm or excited. Weigh growers and breeding stock regularly on a kitchen or hanging scale and record weights. If you call the vet, have ready your records: age, breed, weight changes, feed and any recent changes, when the problem started, droppings and temperature, and how many other rabbits are affected.
firstSteps: Watch each rabbit for a minute before touching it, noting appetite, alertness, posture and breathing, so you learn what is normal for that animal.
Check droppings, leftover feed and water every day, because a drop in eating or droppings is often the very first sign of trouble.
Move any rabbit that looks unwell into a clean, quiet, shaded hutch away from the others, with fresh hay and water close by.
Keep the sick rabbit cool in hot weather and out of draughts and rain in cold or wet weather.
Record the date, what you saw, the temperature if you took it, and any feed or weather changes, so the vet has clear information.
Wash your hands after handling rabbits, especially any with skin problems or discharge, and clean equipment between hutches.
Call your vet or animal health assistant the same day if a rabbit stops eating or passing droppings; do not give any medicines without veterinary advice.
detail.vetTreatment: Routine vet care keeps a rabbit unit healthy and profitable. A vet or animal health officer can do a whole-herd health check, looking at housing, ventilation, feeding, hygiene and record keeping, and advise on improvements. They can check teeth, body condition, skin, ears and feet, and examine breeding does and bucks before mating. Coccidiosis, mange and ear mites, and snuffles (a breathing infection often linked to Pasteurella bacteria) are among the common problems on Kenyan farms, and your vet can advise on prevention plans and, if needed, prescribe treatment. Ask your vet which rabbit vaccines, if any, are available and recommended in your area, because availability in Kenya is limited and changes over time. Faecal (dung) tests help decide whether parasite treatment is needed, instead of treating blindly. Any medicine, including anticoccidials, antibiotics and anti-parasite drugs, must be prescribed by a vet, because rabbits react badly to some drugs used in other animals, and some antibiotics given by mouth can upset their gut bacteria and cause fatal diarrhoea. Using antibiotics only when truly needed also slows antimicrobial resistance, where germs stop responding to medicines. If rabbits are kept for meat, always follow the meat withdrawal period on the label or given by the vet before slaughter or sale.
prevention: Give unlimited clean, dry hay or dry grass every day as the main part of the diet, because fibre protects the gut and wears down the teeth.
Add fresh greens such as clean sukuma wiki, lucerne, sweet potato vines or other safe forages, introducing anything new slowly and avoiding wet, wilted, fermenting or mouldy greens.
Feed rabbit pellets in measured amounts rather than filling the feeder, as too many pellets and starchy kitchen waste can upset the gut and cause obesity.
Provide clean water at all times in a drinker or heavy bowl, and clean drinkers often to stop slime and germs building up.
Build or raise hutches off the ground in a shaded, well-ventilated spot, protect them from rain, and clean out droppings and wet bedding regularly to cut coccidiosis and ammonia.
Avoid overcrowding, give each rabbit enough space to stretch and hop, and separate bucks and growing rabbits as needed to prevent fighting.
Quarantine new or returning rabbits for about two to three weeks, check them for mites, discharge and diarrhoea, and buy only from healthy, reputable sources.
Keep good records of births, weaning, weights, feed, illness and treatments, and plan regular checks with your vet or animal health officer.
detail.impact: Healthy rabbits grow quickly, breed well and give a reliable income from meat, breeding stock, manure and urine sold as fertiliser. Does can produce several litters a year, so a doe that stays healthy is very valuable. Because rabbits hide illness and can deteriorate within a day, small farms in Kenya often lose animals that could have been saved if a change in appetite or droppings had been noticed early. Losses at weaning from diarrhoea and coccidiosis, poor growth from bad feeding, and failed breeding from heat stress or poor condition all cut profit. A few minutes of daily checking, good feeding and clean housing usually cost far less than replacing dead stock, buying medicines, or losing a buyer's trust. Regular weighing and records also show which does and bucks perform best, helping you improve your herd over time.
detail.humanHealth: Healthy, well-kept rabbits pose little risk to people, but good hygiene still matters. Rabbits with skin problems can sometimes carry ringworm (a fungal infection) or mites that can cause an itchy rash in people, and scratches or bites can become infected. Wear gloves when handling rabbits with skin lesions, wash hands with soap after handling rabbits, cleaning hutches or collecting manure and urine, and keep children supervised. If rabbits have been treated with medicines, follow the meat withdrawal period so no drug residues reach consumers.
detail.outlook: Rabbits that are well fed, kept in clean, cool, dry housing and checked daily usually stay healthy and productive for several years. The main danger is that rabbits hide illness, so problems are often found late. When a change such as reduced eating, fewer droppings, discharge or hunching is noticed early and a vet is called promptly, the chances of recovery are much better. Rabbits that go a day or more without eating or passing droppings, or that are badly heat stressed, have a much poorer outlook. Knowing what normal looks like for each of your rabbits is the single best way to protect them.

faqs.q: Is it normal for my rabbit to eat its own droppings?
faqs.a: Yes. Rabbits eat special soft droppings called caecotrophs, usually at night or early morning, straight from the bottom. These carry vitamins and protein made by gut bacteria and are essential for health. The hard, round droppings you see in the hutch are not normally eaten. If you find lots of uneaten soft droppings stuck to the bottom or lying in the hutch, the diet may have too little fibre or the rabbit may be too fat or sore to reach, so check feeding and ask your vet.

faqs.q: My rabbit's urine is red or orange. Is it bleeding?
faqs.a: Often not. Pigments from plants and some greens can turn normal rabbit urine yellow, orange, red or brown, and extra calcium can make it cloudy. If the rabbit is eating, drinking and behaving normally, it is usually fine. Call the vet if you see clear blood spots or clots, straining, a wet or burnt-looking bottom, or if the rabbit is dull or off its food.

faqs.q: How long can a rabbit go without eating?
faqs.a: Not long. A rabbit that stops eating or stops passing droppings can develop a dangerous gut slowdown within hours. If a rabbit has eaten little or nothing, or has passed few or no droppings, for around 12 hours, treat it as an emergency and call your vet the same day. Do not wait to see if it improves overnight.

faqs.q: How do I know if my rabbit is too thin or too fat?
faqs.a: Run your hand along the spine and over the hips and ribs. In a rabbit in good condition you can feel the bones under a thin, even layer of flesh. If the bones feel sharp and prominent, the rabbit is too thin. If you cannot feel the ribs or spine at all, and there are fat rolls, it is too fat. Weighing your rabbits regularly and writing it down helps you spot slow weight loss that you might not see.

faqs.q: Do rabbits still need water if they eat lots of greens?
faqs.a: Yes. Greens contain some water, but rabbits need clean, fresh drinking water at all times, especially nursing does, growing rabbits and all rabbits in hot weather. Lack of water slows the gut, reduces appetite and milk production, and makes heat stress much worse. Check drinkers twice a day, because they can block, leak or get knocked over.

faqs.q: How often should I check my rabbits?
faqs.a: Look at every rabbit at least twice a day, usually at morning and evening feeding, checking appetite, droppings, water and behaviour. Do a quick hands-on check of eyes, nose, ears, teeth, coat, feet and bottom about once a week, and weigh growers and breeding stock regularly. Ask your vet or animal health officer to visit for a herd health check from time to time, and whenever you notice a problem in more than one rabbit.

healthy.imagePrompt: A healthy, alert New Zealand White rabbit sitting upright in a clean, shaded wooden hutch, ears up, bright clear eyes and clean nose, smooth white coat, nibbling fresh hay with a few round dry droppings visible on the floor, soft natural daylight.
healthy.seoDescription: Healthy rabbit guide for Kenyan farmers: bright eyes, clean nose, round droppings, steady hay appetite, normal 38.5–40 °C temperature and early warning signs.

card.headline: Pot-bellied, thin young rabbits with diarrhoea
card.look: Weaned rabbits, usually 4 to 12 weeks old, stop growing, look rough-coated and bony along the back, and have swollen bellies. The droppings turn soft, pasty or watery, and the fur around the tail is often soiled.
card.action: Separate sick rabbits, clean droppings out of every cage today, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer to confirm coccidiosis and prescribe the right anticoccidial medicine.

aka: Kuhara kwa sungura (diarrhoea in rabbits, general Swahili description)
detail.summary: Coccidiosis is a gut and liver disease of rabbits caused by tiny single-celled parasites called Eimeria. It is one of the most common reasons young rabbits stop growing, develop pot bellies and die in the weeks after weaning. Almost every rabbitry carries some of these parasites, so the disease is really about how many the rabbits swallow, which depends on hygiene, cage design and stress. With good cleaning, raised wire floors, clean feeding and prompt vet treatment, losses can be greatly reduced.
detail.cause: The disease is caused by several species of Eimeria, which are protozoa (microscopic single-celled parasites, not worms and not bacteria). Each Eimeria species infects only one kind of animal, so the types that attack rabbits do not infect chickens, goats or people, and the chicken types do not infect rabbits. There are two main forms. In the intestinal form, several species, including Eimeria flavescens and Eimeria intestinalis, which are among the most harmful, invade the lining of the small intestine, caecum and large intestine. They multiply inside the gut cells and burst out, destroying the lining. The damaged gut cannot absorb food and water well, so the rabbit gets diarrhoea, loses fluids and wastes away, and harmful gut bacteria can take over and make things worse. In the liver form, Eimeria stiedae travels from the gut to the liver and multiplies in the bile ducts, the small tubes that carry bile from the liver. The bile ducts swell and become blocked, the liver enlarges, and the belly swells. Liver-form rabbits may look only slightly ill but grow very poorly, and heavy infections can kill. Many rabbits carry mixed infections of both forms at the same time.
spread: Infected rabbits pass huge numbers of microscopic eggs called oocysts in their droppings, often without looking very sick themselves.
Freshly passed oocysts are not yet infective; they need about one to a few days in warm, damp conditions to mature, which is why droppings left lying in cages, trays and bedding are so dangerous.
Rabbits become infected by swallowing mature oocysts in feed, greens, hay or water that has touched droppings, for example pellets or grass thrown on a dirty cage floor.
Wooden or solid-floored hutches where droppings collect, and colony pens on soil, allow oocysts to build up to very high numbers.
Greens cut from ground where rabbit droppings or manure have been spread, or from around the rabbit house, can carry oocysts into the cage.
Oocysts survive for months in moist, shaded places and resist many common disinfectants, so a dirty unit can keep infecting batch after batch of young rabbits.
Stress at weaning, sudden feed changes, overcrowding, transport, heat, cold and wet weather lower resistance and often trigger outbreaks.
Contaminated equipment, feeders, drinkers, shoes and hands can carry oocysts between cages and between farms, as can newly bought rabbits that are carrying the parasite.
detail.atRisk: Young rabbits from weaning to about three months of age are most at risk, with the worst losses usually seen a few weeks after weaning, when they lose the protection of their mother's milk and are stressed by separation and new feed. Adult rabbits are usually partly immune and often show no signs, but they keep shedding oocysts and infecting the young ones; does that are pregnant, nursing, old or sick can still become ill. All breeds are affected, including New Zealand White, California, Chinchilla, Flemish Giant and local crosses. Risk is highest in rabbitries with solid wooden floors, rabbits kept on the ground or in deep litter, overcrowded cages, feeding on the floor, and poor cleaning routines. Outbreaks are often more common during the long and short rains, when damp, warm conditions help oocysts mature and survive. Growing meat-rabbit enterprises with frequent batches of weaners are especially affected if cages are not cleaned between batches.

early: Young rabbits eat less than usual and stop gaining weight, so they look smaller than litter mates of the same age.
The coat becomes dull, rough and stary instead of smooth and shiny.
Droppings become softer, pasty or clumped together instead of firm, round, separate pellets, and may contain mucus.
Soiling of the fur around the tail and hind legs with soft droppings.
Rabbits are quieter than normal, sit hunched in a corner and are slower to come to the feeder.
The belly starts to look fuller or rounder than normal while the back and hips feel thin when you run your hand along them.
advanced: Watery or mucus-covered diarrhoea, sometimes with streaks of blood, and a strong sour smell in the cage.
A clearly swollen pot belly, especially in the liver form, while the spine and hip bones stick out.
Severe weight loss and wasting, with sunken eyes and skin that stays tented when gently pinched, showing dehydration.
Grinding of teeth, which often signals pain, and refusal of all feed and water.
In the liver form, the whites of the eyes or inside of the ears may look yellowish (jaundice), and the rabbit becomes weak.
Rabbits lying stretched out or on their side, too weak to move, sometimes with paddling or fits shortly before death.
Deaths of several young rabbits over days to weeks, often while older rabbits in the same unit look healthy.

lookalikes.name: Mucoid enteropathy (part of the enteritis complex)
lookalikes.howToTell: Affected rabbits pass large amounts of clear, jelly-like mucus, often with little or no normal droppings, and the belly may be bloated and sloshing with fluid. Coccidiosis usually causes pasty or watery diarrhoea and slow wasting. The two often occur together, so only a faecal test or post-mortem by a vet can separate them.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (Clostridium infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a sudden, fast-killing diarrhoea, often brown and watery with a foul smell, frequently after a sudden feed change or too much starchy feed and too little fibre. Rabbits may die within a day or two, sometimes without much diarrhoea at all. Coccidiosis usually builds up more slowly, with weight loss and pot bellies over days to weeks.

lookalikes.name: Colibacillosis (E. coli diarrhoea)
lookalikes.howToTell: E. coli often hits very young kits still in the nest, causing yellowish watery diarrhoea and high deaths in whole litters, as well as weaners. Coccidiosis is most common after weaning. A vet needs lab tests to tell them apart, and mixed infections are common.

lookalikes.name: Tapeworm cysts (Cysticercus pisiformis) and other liver problems
lookalikes.howToTell: At post-mortem, tapeworm cysts look like small fluid-filled bubbles on the liver surface and in the belly, and come from rabbits eating greens contaminated by dog droppings. Liver coccidiosis shows firm white or cream-coloured spots and swollen tubes inside the liver tissue. Live rabbits with tapeworm cysts often show few signs, so a vet post-mortem is the best way to tell.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects coccidiosis from the history: young rabbits after weaning, diarrhoea, pot bellies, poor growth and deaths, together with the cage conditions. To confirm it, the vet or lab examines fresh droppings under a microscope using a flotation test, which floats the oocysts up so they can be seen and counted. Because healthy rabbits often carry a few oocysts, the number found and the signs in the animals both matter; a heavy count in sick young rabbits strongly points to coccidiosis. A post-mortem (examination of a dead rabbit) is often the clearest test. In the liver form the liver is enlarged with firm white to yellowish spots and thickened bile ducts, and in the intestinal form the gut wall is thickened, inflamed, sometimes with white spots, and the contents are watery. The lab can also check for other causes such as E. coli, Clostridium or mucoid enteropathy, which often occur alongside coccidiosis. To help, the farmer can collect fresh droppings from several affected rabbits into a clean, sealed container or bag, label it, keep it cool (not frozen) and get it to the vet or lab within a day. A rabbit that has just died should be kept cool in a sealed bag and taken quickly to the vet, the County Veterinary Office or a veterinary laboratory such as those run by the Directorate of Veterinary Services or KALRO. Write down the ages of affected rabbits, when signs started, how many have died, recent feed changes, and any medicines already given.
firstSteps: Move rabbits with diarrhoea, pot bellies or weakness into a separate clean cage, away from healthy stock, and handle them last.
Remove all droppings, wet bedding and spilled feed from every cage, tray and floor today, and keep doing this daily, because oocysts become infective within a few days.
Make sure every rabbit has constant access to clean, fresh drinking water in a clean drinker that droppings cannot fall into, as diarrhoea quickly causes dehydration.
Feed good-quality hay or dry grass and fresh, clean greens from areas free of rabbit droppings and manure, and avoid sudden changes or large amounts of wet, lush feed.
Never put feed or greens on the cage floor; use raised racks, hay nets or feeders so food cannot touch droppings.
Keep sick rabbits warm, dry, out of draughts and out of direct sun, and reduce stress by not moving, mixing or transporting them.
Wash your hands after handling sick rabbits and droppings, and clean boots, feeders and tools before going to the healthy cages.

Record the ages, number sick, number dead and dates, keep a fresh rabbit or droppings sample cool, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer; do not give any drugs until a vet has confirmed the cause and prescribed treatment.
detail.vetTreatment: Coccidiosis is caused by a parasite, so ordinary antibiotics alone do not cure it; the vet will prescribe a specific anticoccidial medicine. Commonly used options in rabbits include sulfonamide drugs such as sulfadimethoxine or sulfaquinoxaline, often given in drinking water, and newer anticoccidials such as toltrazuril or diclazuril. Amprolium is also used in some places, though its effect in rabbits varies. Because the whole group is usually exposed, the vet will often recommend treating all rabbits in the affected unit, not only the sick ones. The choice of drug, dose and length of treatment depend on the product, the form of the disease and local availability, so these must be decided by a vet and not guessed from chicken or livestock labels, as some poultry products and doses are unsafe or ineffective in rabbits. Sulfonamides are antimicrobial drugs, so use them only on prescription and finish the course exactly as directed, to slow the development of drug resistance in both parasites and bacteria. If bacteria have also invaded the damaged gut, the vet may add an antibiotic, again only where truly needed. Supportive care is just as important: fluids for dehydrated rabbits, good hay and fibre to restore normal gut movement, warmth and quiet. Very weak rabbits may not survive even with treatment, and liver damage can leave some survivors as poor growers. All drugs used in meat rabbits have withdrawal periods, a set time after the last treatment before the rabbit can be slaughtered for food, so follow the withdrawal time on the label and the vet's instructions. Treatment must be combined with deep cleaning of cages, otherwise rabbits are quickly reinfected.
prevention: Keep rabbits in raised cages with wire mesh floors of a suitable size, so droppings fall through and away from the rabbits; if you use wooden hutches, fit mesh floors or removable trays that you clean often.
Remove droppings from under and inside cages at least daily or every other day, before oocysts have time to mature, and never let manure pile up close to the cages.
Feed pellets and grains in raised feeders or hoppers and hay in racks, never on the floor, and use drinkers or nipple systems that cannot be soiled with droppings.

Cut greens from clean areas, not from where rabbit manure is spread or near the rabbit house, and do not let dogs foul the cutting area; let washed greens wilt slightly rather than feeding them soaking wet.

Between batches, empty cages completely, scrub off all droppings, then use boiling water, a blowlamp on metal mesh, or a disinfectant your vet or agrovet confirms works against coccidia, and let cages dry fully in the sun before restocking; many ordinary disinfectants do not kill oocysts.
Avoid overcrowding, wean rabbits gradually, keep litters together after weaning where possible, and make feed changes slowly over about a week to reduce stress.
Feed a balanced diet rich in fibre with enough protein, minerals and vitamins, as well-nourished rabbits resist and recover from coccidiosis better.
Ask your vet about preventive anticoccidial feeds or planned treatment programmes for weaners on farms with repeated outbreaks, and follow withdrawal periods for meat rabbits.
Quarantine new rabbits in a separate cage for at least two to three weeks, check their droppings, and buy breeding stock from clean, well-managed rabbitries.
Keep the rabbit house dry and well ventilated, especially during the long and short rains, and fix leaking roofs and drainage.
detail.impact: Coccidiosis is one of the biggest hidden costs in Kenyan rabbit farming. Deaths of weaners after weaning can wipe out much of a batch in badly affected units, but even rabbits that survive often grow slowly and reach market weight weeks late, eating feed without giving a good return. Liver-form rabbits may look acceptable but have damaged livers that are condemned at slaughter, and thin carcasses fetch lower prices from buyers, hotels and butcheries. Farmers spend money on medicines, vet visits and extra labour for cleaning. Repeated outbreaks can make a rabbit enterprise look unprofitable and discourage new farmers who started with breeding stock and cages. Breeding units that sell weaners can lose their reputation if buyers' rabbits fall sick soon after purchase. On the positive side, most of these losses can be prevented with good cage design and hygiene, which cost far less than repeated deaths.
detail.humanHealth: The Eimeria parasites that cause rabbit coccidiosis infect only rabbits and are not known to infect people. However, diarrhoeic droppings can carry other germs, so wash your hands with soap after handling sick rabbits, droppings or bedding, and keep children from playing with sick animals. The bigger human-health concern is drug residues: meat from rabbits treated with sulfonamides or other anticoccidials must not be eaten or sold until the withdrawal period on the label or advised by your vet has passed. Do not slaughter visibly sick rabbits for food, and discard livers with white spots or obvious damage.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early the disease is caught, how heavy the infection is, and how quickly the environment is cleaned. Rabbits treated in the early stages, while still eating and drinking, often recover well, and the rest of the group can be protected by vet-guided treatment and strict hygiene. Rabbits that are already severely dehydrated, refusing food or lying on their side have a poor chance even with treatment. Survivors of heavy liver infections may remain poor growers because of liver damage, and some are better culled than kept for breeding. Recovered rabbits develop some immunity to the species that infected them, but they can still carry and shed oocysts, so prevention must continue. Farms that fix floors, feeding and cleaning routines usually see far fewer and milder outbreaks.

faqs.q: My adult rabbits look healthy. Why do only the young ones get sick and die?
faqs.a: Adult rabbits have usually met the parasite before and built up partial immunity, so they often show no signs. But they still pass oocysts in their droppings. Young rabbits after weaning have no immunity yet, are stressed by weaning and new feed, and swallow oocysts from the cage, so they get the full disease. That is why cleaning and good cage design matter most around weaning time.

faqs.q: Can I use the coccidiosis medicine I bought for my chickens?
faqs.a: Do not do this without asking a vet. The coccidia in chickens are different species from those in rabbits, and some poultry products or the doses on poultry labels are not suitable or safe for rabbits. Some drugs that work in chickens work poorly in rabbits. Your vet will choose a product and dose that is right for rabbits and tell you the meat withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Will antibiotics cure coccidiosis?
faqs.a: Ordinary antibiotics do not kill the coccidia parasite. The medicines that work are anticoccidials, and some of these, such as sulfonamides, also happen to be antimicrobials. A vet may sometimes add an antibiotic if bacteria have invaded the damaged gut. Using antibiotics without a proper diagnosis wastes money, can upset the rabbit's delicate gut and helps drug resistance develop.

faqs.q: Rabbits eat their own soft droppings at night. Does that spread the disease?
faqs.a: Rabbits naturally eat special soft droppings called caecotrophs straight from the bottom; this is normal and needed for good digestion. Newly passed oocysts are not yet infective, so this habit is not the main problem. The danger comes from ordinary droppings left lying in the cage for a day or more, where the oocysts mature and then get onto feed, greens and drinkers. Removing droppings regularly breaks this cycle.

faqs.q: Is it safe to eat rabbits from a group that had coccidiosis?
faqs.a: Rabbit coccidiosis does not infect people. Rabbits that are healthy and well-grown at slaughter can be eaten, but only after the withdrawal period of any medicine they were given has fully passed. Do not slaughter sick or wasted rabbits for food, and throw away any liver with white spots or swollen ducts, which is a sign of liver coccidiosis.

faqs.q: How do I clean cages properly after an outbreak?
faqs.a: First remove all rabbits, droppings, bedding and leftover feed. Scrub every surface with water and soap or detergent to remove dirt, because disinfectants do not work through dirt. Oocysts resist many common disinfectants, so use boiling water, carefully flame metal wire mesh with a blowlamp, or use a product your vet or agrovet confirms kills coccidia. Clean feeders and drinkers the same way, then let everything dry fully in the sun before bringing rabbits back.

products.role: Coccidiosis damages the gut lining and, in the liver form, the liver, where vitamin A is stored, so recovering rabbits may benefit from vitamin A, D3 and E support. Used only as your vet advises, AD3E can help correct a vitamin shortfall and support normal recovery of the gut lining and general condition alongside vet-prescribed anticoccidial treatment, good fibre-rich feeding and strict cage hygiene. It does not kill the parasite or cure coccidiosis.

coccidiosis.imagePrompt: A realistic photo of a thin young white rabbit with a noticeably swollen pot belly, rough dull coat and soiled fur around the tail, sitting hunched in a raised wire-mesh rabbit cage in a simple Kenyan rabbit house.
coccidiosis.seoDescription: Rabbit coccidiosis: spot diarrhoea, pot belly and weight loss in weaners, act fast before the vet arrives, and prevent it with hygiene and wire floors.

card.headline: Thick white discharge and crusty front paws
card.look: The rabbit sneezes and snorts, with thick white or yellow mucus around the nostrils. The fur on the inner side of the front paws is wet, matted or crusty from wiping the nose.
card.action: Move the sneezing rabbit to a clean, airy, separate hutch away from the others, then call your vet before it spreads or gets worse.

aka: Wry neck or head tilt (when the ear is affected)
detail.summary: Snuffles is a bacterial infection of the nose, sinuses and airways of rabbits, caused mainly by Pasteurella multocida. It starts with sneezing and a thick white nasal discharge but can spread to the lungs, eyes, ears, womb and under the skin as abscesses (pockets of pus). Many rabbits carry the germ quietly and fall sick when stressed, so one sick rabbit usually means others in the unit carry it too. It is one of the most common reasons for poor growth, failed breeding and losses on Kenyan rabbit farms.
detail.cause: The cause is a bacterium called Pasteurella multocida, sometimes with other germs such as Bordetella bronchiseptica or Staphylococcus joining in. Many healthy-looking rabbits carry Pasteurella deep in the nose without showing signs; these are called carriers. When the rabbit's defences drop, from ammonia fumes from urine, dust, poor ventilation, crowding, heat, cold draughts, transport, kindling (giving birth) or weaning, the bacteria multiply and inflame the lining of the nose and sinuses. This causes sneezing and pus-like discharge. Because the nose connects to the tear ducts, the middle ear and the windpipe, the infection can travel to the eyes (sticky, weepy eyes), the ear (head tilt and loss of balance), and the lungs (pneumonia). The bacteria can also be carried in the blood or through bites and wounds to form abscesses under the skin, in the jaw, or in the reproductive organs, causing womb infections in does and swollen testicles in bucks. Rabbit pus is very thick, like cream cheese, so abscesses do not burst and drain easily. Once a rabbit has had snuffles, the germ often stays hidden in its sinuses for life and can flare up again.
spread: Direct nose-to-nose contact between rabbits, especially when they share a hutch or touch through wire walls.
Droplets sneezed into the air, which travel short distances between hutches that are close together in a poorly ventilated house.
Shared feeders, water bowls, nipple drinkers and hay that sick rabbits have sneezed on or soiled.
From doe to kits around kindling and during nursing, which is why infected does often produce sickly litters.
During mating, when bucks and does are put together; an infected buck can spread it to many does.
Bringing in new breeding stock from markets or other farms without quarantine, since carriers look healthy.
On the hands, clothes and equipment of people moving between hutches or farms.

Stress triggers such as ammonia smell from dirty urine trays, dusty hay or sawdust, overcrowding, hot iron-sheet roofs, cold night draughts during the rains, and long journeys turn silent carriers into sick rabbits.
detail.atRisk: All rabbits can get snuffles, but the highest risk is in weaners (just after weaning), does around kindling and while nursing, and older breeding stock that have carried the germ for a long time. Rabbits kept in closed, poorly ventilated houses or hutches where urine collects and smells of ammonia are at great risk, as are units that are overcrowded or mix rabbits from different sources. Cases often rise during the cold, damp long and short rains when farmers close up houses and air goes stale, and during hot dry spells under iron roofs. Farms that buy breeding stock from markets or several different breeders, and those without a quarantine hutch, see more outbreaks. Both meat breeds such as New Zealand White and California and local crosses are affected; no breed is truly resistant.

early: Sneezing, often several times in a row, and snorting or snuffling sounds when breathing.
Clear watery nasal discharge that soon becomes thick, white, cream or yellow.
Wet, matted or crusty fur on the inner side of the front paws and legs, because rabbits wipe their nose with their paws.
Watery or sticky eyes, sometimes with white pus in the corner of the eye and wet fur below it.
Rubbing the face against the cage wire or floor.
Slightly reduced appetite and less interest in pellets, while still drinking.
advanced: Noisy, laboured breathing, breathing with the mouth open, or flaring nostrils, which suggests the lungs are involved (pneumonia) and is an emergency.
Head tilt (wry neck), rolling, circling or falling over, caused by infection spreading to the middle and inner ear.
Firm or soft lumps under the skin, on the jaw, face, neck or chest, which are abscesses full of thick pus.
Weight loss, a bony back, dull rough coat and refusing food.
In does, a smelly or bloody discharge from the vulva, failed pregnancies or small, weak litters; in bucks, swollen testicles.
Sudden death with few signs, especially in young rabbits, when the bacteria reach the blood (septicaemia).

lookalikes.name: Dental disease (overgrown teeth or tooth root problems)
lookalikes.howToTell: Rabbits with tooth problems drool, have a wet chin, drop food, lose weight and may have overgrown front teeth you can see. Long tooth roots can block tear ducts and cause eye and nose discharge on one side, but there is usually less sneezing. A vet checks the teeth and may X-ray the skull.

lookalikes.name: Dust or irritant sneezing
lookalikes.howToTell: Sneezing after fresh dusty hay, sawdust or ammonia fumes is sudden, the discharge stays clear and watery, and the rabbit eats normally. It settles within a day or two once bedding is changed and ventilation improved. Thick white pus and matted paws point to infection instead.

lookalikes.name: Encephalitozoon cuniculi (a parasite affecting the brain and kidneys)
lookalikes.howToTell: This parasite also causes head tilt, rolling and weakness, but usually without any history of sneezing or nasal discharge. Ear infection from Pasteurella often comes with snuffles signs or pus in the ear. A vet may need blood tests or X-rays to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Ear mites (ear canker)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ear mites cause thick, brown-grey, flaky crusts inside the ear flap, intense scratching and head shaking. You can see the crusts by looking into the ear. Pasteurella ear infection is deeper inside the head, so the outer ear often looks clean while the rabbit tilts its head.

detail.diagnosis: A vet usually suspects snuffles from the signs and the farm history. They will examine the nose, eyes, ears, teeth, chest and body for abscesses, listen to the lungs and check the reproductive organs. To confirm the germ and choose an antibiotic that works, the vet may take a deep nasal swab or a sample of pus for culture and sensitivity testing at a laboratory such as the Central Veterinary Laboratories at Kabete or a county or regional veterinary lab. X-rays can show pneumonia, ear damage or tooth root problems. When a rabbit dies, a post-mortem (examination of the body) is very useful for the whole herd, showing pus in the sinuses, lungs, ears or womb. To help, the farmer should note how many rabbits are sick, their ages, when signs started, recent purchases or shows, any recent stress like transport or a heat spell, and any drugs already given. If a rabbit dies, keep the body cool in a sealed bag (chilled, not frozen) and take it to the vet within a day.
firstSteps: Isolate every sneezing rabbit in a separate hutch, ideally in a different room or at the far end of the house, and handle it last after the healthy ones.
Improve air flow immediately: open vents and windows during the day while avoiding cold draughts on the rabbits at night, and remove anything that blocks fresh air.
Clean out urine trays and soiled bedding today so there is no ammonia smell, and replace dusty hay or sawdust with clean, dust-free bedding.

Make sure the rabbit has constant clean, fresh water and its usual hay, greens and pellets; offer favourite fresh greens to keep it eating, because rabbits that stop eating can quickly develop serious gut problems.
Gently wipe the nose and eyes with a clean cloth dipped in cooled boiled water, using a fresh piece for each rabbit, and wash your hands afterwards.
Keep the rabbit calm, in shade, out of the sun and rain, and avoid handling, mating, transporting or selling it.
Stop all movement of rabbits in and out of the unit, stop mating, and do not bring in new stock until the vet has advised.

Write down which rabbits are affected, their signs, and the date, and call your vet or County Veterinary Officer; treat laboured breathing, head tilt or a rabbit that has stopped eating as urgent, and do not give any drugs until the vet has prescribed them.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet. Snuffles is bacterial, so the vet will usually prescribe an antibiotic, often as an injection or in water, chosen for safety in rabbits. Drugs commonly used include fluoroquinolones such as enrofloxacin, potentiated sulphonamides (trimethoprim-sulpha) and tetracyclines such as oxytetracycline, ideally guided by a culture and sensitivity test. It is very important that farmers never give rabbits antibiotics meant for other animals without vet advice: some, such as oral penicillins, amoxicillin, ampicillin, lincomycin and clindamycin, can upset the rabbit's gut bacteria and cause fatal diarrhoea. Courses for snuffles are often longer than for other animals, and stopping early or using the wrong drug encourages antimicrobial resistance, where the germs no longer respond, so finish the full course exactly as prescribed and never use antibiotics just to prevent disease. The vet may add pain relief and anti-inflammatory drugs, eye drops or ointment for infected eyes, steam or nebulisation to loosen mucus, and assisted feeding for rabbits that stop eating. Abscesses usually need surgical removal or opening and flushing by a vet, because the thick pus does not drain well, and antibiotics alone rarely clear them. Rabbits with head tilt may need long treatment and nursing, and some never fully straighten. For meat rabbits, the vet will tell you the meat withdrawal period, the time you must wait after the last dose before slaughtering, so that no drug residues reach consumers. Expect that signs may improve but the germ often stays hidden, so relapses are common; the vet may advise culling chronic or repeatedly sick breeding rabbits to protect the herd.
prevention: Buy breeding stock only from clean, well-run farms that have no sneezing rabbits, and avoid buying from markets where rabbits from many sources are mixed.
Quarantine every new rabbit in a separate hutch away from the main unit for at least two to three weeks, watching closely for sneezing, discharge or matted paws before mixing.
Provide good ventilation without draughts: raise hutches off the ground, leave open mesh sides or vents high up, and avoid closing the house up tightly during the rains.
Clean urine trays and remove droppings often, ideally daily in busy units, so the house never smells of ammonia; use slatted or wire floors and dry, dust-free bedding.
Avoid overcrowding, keep one adult per hutch, give each rabbit enough space, and separate weaners into small groups rather than large crowded pens.
Reduce stress: shade hutches from midday sun, insulate under iron roofs, handle rabbits gently, and plan transport for cool times of day.
Feed a balanced diet with plenty of good hay or fodder, clean greens and quality pellets, plus constant clean water, so the immune system stays strong.
Check every rabbit's nose, eyes and front paws weekly and before mating; never mate a sneezing rabbit, and consider culling breeding stock that keep relapsing, as they keep infecting kits.
Clean and disinfect hutches, feeders and drinkers between occupants, and work from young and healthy rabbits to old and sick ones.
Commercial Pasteurella vaccines for rabbits exist in some countries but are not widely available in Kenya; ask your vet about current options, and rely mainly on management and biosecurity.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan rabbit farm, snuffles quietly eats into profits. Sick weaners grow slowly and take longer to reach slaughter weight, so feed costs rise per kilo of meat sold. Does with chronic infection may fail to conceive, abort, or produce small litters of weak kits that die young, cutting the number of rabbits for sale. Pneumonia can kill rabbits quickly, and abscesses or head tilt make rabbits unfit for sale. Buyers of breeding stock and rabbit associations often refuse rabbits with runny noses or matted paws, damaging a farm's reputation. Vet visits, drugs and the cost of replacing culled breeding stock add up, and meat cannot be sold during drug withdrawal periods. Because the germ spreads through the whole unit, one neglected case can turn into a long-running herd problem.
detail.humanHealth: Pasteurella multocida can occasionally infect people, usually through bites or scratches, causing a painful, swollen, red wound infection within a day or two. The risk from rabbits is low compared with cats and dogs, but children, elderly people, pregnant women and anyone with a weak immune system should take care. Wash hands with soap after handling rabbits, wear gloves when cleaning discharge or abscesses, and clean any bite or scratch well with soap and running water. See a doctor if a wound becomes swollen, hot or very painful, and mention you keep rabbits. Only slaughter meat rabbits after the drug withdrawal period has passed, so that no antibiotic residues reach your family or customers.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how early treatment starts and which parts of the body are affected. Mild, early snuffles often improves well with the right vet-prescribed antibiotic and better housing, although the rabbit may remain a carrier and flare up later under stress. Long-standing nasal infection is hard to clear completely because the germ hides in the sinus bones. Rabbits with pneumonia have a guarded to poor outlook and can die quickly, especially young ones. Head tilt may improve over weeks, and many rabbits learn to cope, but some stay tilted for life. Abscesses often return unless fully removed. Good ventilation, low stress, strong nutrition and culling chronic carriers give the herd the best long-term chance.

faqs.q: Will snuffles go away on its own if I just wait?
faqs.a: Sometimes a very mild case seems to settle, but usually the infection keeps going and slowly spreads to the eyes, ears or lungs, and to other rabbits. Waiting often means a harder, longer treatment later. Isolate the rabbit, fix the housing and call your vet early.

faqs.q: Can I use the antibiotic I bought for my chickens or cows?
faqs.a: No, not without your vet's advice. Rabbits have a delicate gut, and some common antibiotics, especially penicillin-type drugs and some others given by mouth, can cause deadly diarrhoea in rabbits. The wrong drug or a short course also builds antibiotic resistance. Let a vet choose a rabbit-safe drug and the right course.

faqs.q: Why does my rabbit keep getting sick again after treatment?
faqs.a: Pasteurella often hides deep in the sinuses, where antibiotics cannot fully reach it, so the rabbit stays a carrier. Stress such as ammonia smell, heat, cold draughts, kindling or transport lets it flare up again. Improving ventilation, cleaning urine daily and reducing crowding helps most; repeatedly sick breeding rabbits may need to be culled.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell meat from a rabbit that had snuffles?
faqs.a: A rabbit that has recovered can be eaten, but only after the full meat withdrawal period of any drug it received, which your vet will tell you. Do not slaughter rabbits with abscesses, fever, pneumonia or obvious illness for food. Ask your vet or meat inspector if unsure.

faqs.q: Is there a vaccine against snuffles in Kenya?
faqs.a: Pasteurella vaccines for rabbits are made in some countries, but they are not commonly available in Kenya and do not give complete protection. Ask your vet about what is currently available. For now, clean stock, quarantine, good ventilation and hygiene are the best protection.

faqs.q: Should I keep kits from a doe that has snuffles?
faqs.a: Kits from an infected doe often pick up the germ early in life. If the doe is valuable, your vet may help you plan, but many farmers choose not to keep her kits for breeding and to replace the doe with clean stock. Weaners from her can still be raised for meat if they stay healthy.

snuffles.seoDescription: Snuffles in rabbits: spot sneezing, white nasal discharge and matted front paws early, learn first steps, vet treatment and prevention for Kenyan farms.

card.headline: Thick brown crusts inside the ear
card.look: The rabbit shakes its head, scratches its ears and may let one or both ears droop. Inside the ear you see dry, flaky, grey-brown crusts in layers, like stacked cornflakes, sometimes filling the canal.
card.action: Separate the rabbit, do not pick off the crusts, clean its hutch and call your vet or animal health officer for treatment for every rabbit in contact.

detail.summary: Ear mites are tiny parasites that live inside a rabbit's ear and cause painful, crusty ear canker. It is one of the most common problems in Kenyan rabbit units, especially where rabbits share hutches or are bought from markets without checking. Caught early, it usually responds well to vet-prescribed treatment. Left alone, it causes weight loss, poor breeding, deep ear infections and sometimes a permanent head tilt.
detail.cause: Ear canker is caused by a mite called Psoroptes cuniculi. A mite is a very small relative of ticks and spiders, just visible to the naked eye as a pale moving dot. This mite does not burrow into the skin. It lives on the surface of the skin inside the ear and feeds on tissue fluid. Its feeding and droppings irritate the skin badly. The ear becomes inflamed (red, hot and swollen) and oozes fluid. That fluid dries together with dead skin, mites and mite droppings, building up thick layered grey-brown crusts. The crusts are very itchy and painful, so the rabbit scratches and shakes its head and can wound itself with its hind claws. Bacteria then get into the damaged skin and cause a smelly secondary infection. If the infection travels deeper into the middle and inner ear, it can damage balance and cause a head tilt. In heavy cases the mites spread beyond the ear to the head, face, neck, feet and around the genitals. The whole mite life cycle, from egg to adult, takes roughly three weeks, which is why treatment usually has to continue long enough to kill mites that hatch later.
spread: Direct contact between rabbits is the main route, for example when rabbits share a hutch, when a doe feeds her kits, or during mating.
Newly bought rabbits from markets, neighbours or other farms often bring mites into a clean unit, even when they look healthy at first.
Mites and crust flakes can survive off the rabbit for some days to a few weeks, especially in cool, damp conditions, so dirty bedding, hay, nest boxes and hutch corners can reinfect rabbits.
Shared equipment such as feeders, carry boxes, grooming brushes and transport cages can carry mites and crusts from one hutch to another.
Farmers' hands and clothes can move crust flakes between hutches if they handle an affected rabbit and then a healthy one without washing.
Overcrowding, stress, poor nutrition and other illnesses weaken the rabbit's defences and allow mite numbers to build up quickly.
Some rabbits carry a few mites without signs; stress such as kindling, weaning, transport or a cold wet spell can then trigger an outbreak.
detail.atRisk: Any rabbit of any breed or age can get ear mites. They are seen most in crowded hutches, colony housing and units that buy stock often without quarantine. Young rabbits around and after weaning, pregnant and nursing does, old rabbits and rabbits that are thin or already sick tend to get heavier infestations. Lop-eared breeds may hide early crusts because the ear canal is harder to see. Meat breeds kept in large numbers, such as New Zealand White, Californian, Chinchilla and Flemish Giant crosses, are commonly affected in Kenyan commercial units simply because of the close contact. Cases often rise during the cool, damp months of the long and short rains, when hutches stay wet and mites survive longer in bedding. Wooden hutches with cracks and corners that are hard to clean also hold mites and crusts.

early: Frequent head shaking and flapping of the ears, more than normal grooming.
Scratching at the ears with the hind feet, sometimes followed by the rabbit licking or chewing its feet.
A small amount of light brown or grey waxy flakes at the base of the ear canal when you gently look inside.
Ears that feel warmer than normal and the rabbit pulling away or flinching when you touch them.
Slight hair loss or redness on the inside of the ear flap.
advanced: Thick, dry, grey-brown crusts in layers that fill the ear canal and spread up the inside of the ear flap.
One or both ears drooping or held at an odd angle because of weight of crusts, pain and swelling.
Scratch wounds, scabs and hair loss around the ears, face and neck from the rabbit's own claws.
A bad smell or moist discharge from the ear, suggesting a secondary bacterial infection.
Crusts and hair loss spreading to the head, face, neck, feet or genital area in heavy infestations.
Weight loss, poor appetite, dullness and does that stop breeding or rear weak litters.
Head tilt, circling, rolling or loss of balance if infection has reached the middle or inner ear.

lookalikes.name: Bacterial ear infection or head tilt (often Pasteurella, or the parasite Encephalitozoon cuniculi)
lookalikes.howToTell: These can cause head tilt and loss of balance, but there are usually no thick layered brown crusts in the outer ear. A bacterial ear infection may show creamy pus deep in the canal. A vet may need to examine the ear closely and sometimes run tests to tell them apart, and ear mites can also lead on to a deep infection.

lookalikes.name: Ringworm (a fungal skin infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ringworm causes round, dry, scaly patches of hair loss, often on the face, nose, around the eyes and on the feet, rather than crusts packed inside the ear canal. It can infect people, so wear gloves and get a vet to check it.

lookalikes.name: Fur mites (Cheyletiella, sometimes called 'walking dandruff')
lookalikes.howToTell: Fur mites cause white, dandruff-like scale over the back and shoulders, not crusts in the ear. The flakes may seem to move. They can cause itchy spots on people, unlike ear mites.

lookalikes.name: Normal ear wax or dirt
lookalikes.howToTell: A little light-coloured wax is normal and the rabbit is not bothered. With ear mites the material is thick, layered and crusty, keeps building up, and the rabbit shakes its head, scratches and resents handling.

detail.diagnosis: In most cases a vet or animal health officer can recognise ear canker by looking into the ear and seeing the typical layered brown crusts together with head shaking and scratching. To confirm, they may take a small sample of loose crust from the surface and look at it under a magnifying glass or microscope, where the mites are easy to see. If you place a flake on dark paper in a warm spot you may yourself see tiny pale dots moving. If the rabbit has a head tilt, a smelly discharge or is very ill, the vet will check for deeper ear infection and other diseases, and may take a swab for bacteria. To prepare, keep the rabbit in a clean box, do not remove or wash out the crusts before the visit, note how many rabbits are affected and in which hutches, when signs started, any new rabbits bought recently, and whether rabbits are kept for meat, breeding or both, because this affects which drug is chosen.
firstSteps: Move the affected rabbit to a separate, clean, dry hutch away from the others so mites do not spread further.
Check the ears of every other rabbit, especially those that shared a hutch, nest box or buck, and write down which ones show crusts or head shaking.
Do not pull or scrape off the crusts; the skin underneath is raw and will bleed and hurt, and this does not cure the mites.
Keep the rabbit calm, warm and out of draughts and rain, with fresh clean water and good hay and greens so it keeps eating.
Remove and burn or bury soiled bedding, scrub the hutch, feeders and nest boxes with soapy water, dry them in the sun, and leave the hutch empty if you can.
Wash your hands and change or brush down clothes after handling an affected rabbit, and handle healthy rabbits first and sick ones last.
Do not use dog, cat or livestock sprays, powders, used engine oil, paraffin or home mixtures in the ear; some, such as fipronil sprays sold for dogs and cats, can kill rabbits.
Call your vet, County Veterinary Officer or a trained agrovet animal health officer for a correct diagnosis and a treatment plan for the whole group.
detail.vetTreatment: Ear mites are usually treated with anti-parasite drugs from the avermectin family, such as ivermectin, selamectin or moxidectin, given by injection, by mouth or as a spot-on product, depending on what the vet judges safest for the rabbit. Treatment is normally repeated over several weeks to cover the mite life cycle, because eggs hatch after the first dose. Only a vet should choose the drug and the dose, because rabbits are small and sensitive, and products made for dogs, cats or cattle can easily be overdosed or are simply unsafe for rabbits. All rabbits in contact should usually be treated at the same time, even those without signs, or the problem keeps coming back. The vet may also give pain relief and, if the ear is infected and smelly, an antibiotic or ear treatment. Antibiotics do not kill mites; they are only for a confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infection, and should be used exactly as prescribed to avoid antimicrobial resistance (bacteria learning to survive the drug). As the mites die, the crusts loosen and fall away over one to two weeks; the vet may gently soften them with a safe oil but you should not force them out. For meat rabbits, ask the vet for the meat withdrawal period, which is the time after treatment before a rabbit can safely be slaughtered for food, and keep records of each treated rabbit.
prevention: Quarantine every new rabbit in a separate hutch for at least three to four weeks, check its ears often, and only mix it with your stock when it is clear.
Check the ears of all your rabbits regularly, for example once a week when you feed or clean, so you find the first flakes before crusts build up.
Avoid overcrowding; give each adult rabbit enough space and keep breeding does in their own hutches where possible.
Keep hutches dry, well ventilated and raised off the ground, with a roof that keeps out rain during the long and short rains.
Clean hutches and nest boxes regularly, change bedding often, and scrub and sun-dry hutches thoroughly between litters or before bringing in new rabbits.
Do not share carry boxes, feeders or grooming equipment between farms, and clean them well if they must move between hutches.
Check bucks and does before mating and do not mate a rabbit with crusty ears until it has been treated.
Feed a balanced diet with plenty of good hay, fresh greens and a quality rabbit pellet or mash, with clean water at all times, so rabbits stay strong and resist parasites.
When one case appears, ask your vet whether to treat the whole unit to stop mites moving quietly through the stock.
detail.impact: Ear canker rarely kills rabbits directly, but it quietly eats into farm income. Itchy, sore rabbits eat less and grow slowly, so meat rabbits take longer to reach market weight and fetch lower prices. Breeding does may stop accepting the buck, kindle smaller litters or neglect their kits, and they pass mites on to them. Rabbits with crusty ears, drooping ears or a head tilt are hard to sell as breeding stock, and buyers may avoid a farm that has a reputation for sick rabbits. Treatment costs, vet visits and extra labour add up when the whole unit must be treated, and some severely affected rabbits with permanent balance problems may have to be culled. For a smallholder with a few dozen rabbits, an untreated outbreak can wipe out a season's profit.
detail.humanHealth: The rabbit ear mite Psoroptes cuniculi is not considered a risk to people and does not set up infestation in human ears or skin. Still, wear gloves or wash your hands well after handling crusty ears, because some lookalike conditions such as ringworm and fur mites can infect people. If your rabbits are treated with anti-parasite drugs or antibiotics, follow the meat withdrawal period your vet gives you before slaughtering any treated rabbit for eating or sale, so drug residues do not end up in the meat.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when ear mites are caught early and treated properly. Most rabbits stop scratching within days of the first treatment, and the ears heal over a few weeks once crusts fall away. Recovery is slower when crusts are thick, the skin is badly wounded or a bacterial infection has set in. If infection has reached the middle or inner ear and caused a head tilt, some rabbits recover with vet care but others keep a permanent tilt, though many still eat and live comfortably. The biggest reasons for failure are stopping treatment too early, treating only the rabbit with signs and not its companions, and not cleaning the hutch, which all allow mites to come back.

faqs.q: Can I just clean the crusts out of the ear myself?
faqs.a: No. The crusts are stuck to raw, inflamed skin, and pulling them off is very painful, causes bleeding and does not kill the mites hiding in the ear. Once the vet's treatment kills the mites, the crusts loosen and fall off by themselves over one to two weeks. If the vet advises it, they may show you how to soften them gently, but never force them.

faqs.q: Can I use the dog or cattle spray from the agrovet on my rabbits?
faqs.a: Not without a vet's advice. Some products made for dogs, cats and livestock are dangerous to rabbits; fipronil sprays, for example, have killed rabbits. Even safe ingredients can be overdosed in a small rabbit if you guess the amount from a cattle or dog product. Ask your vet for a rabbit-safe product and the correct dose.

faqs.q: Only one rabbit has crusts. Do I need to treat the others?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Mites spread easily through contact, bedding and nest boxes, and other rabbits may already carry mites without showing signs yet. If you treat only one rabbit, it often gets reinfected from its companions. Your vet will advise whether to treat just the hutch mates or the whole unit, but treating in-contact rabbits together is the normal approach.

faqs.q: How long until I can sell or slaughter a treated rabbit?
faqs.a: That depends on the drug used. Many anti-parasite drugs and antibiotics have a meat withdrawal period, a set number of days when the rabbit must not be slaughtered for food. Ask your vet for the exact period for the product they use, write the treatment date on a record card, and keep those rabbits back until the time is over.

faqs.q: My rabbit now has its head tilted to one side. Is that still ear mites?
faqs.a: It can be. If ear mites are left untreated, infection can spread deep into the ear and affect balance. But head tilt can also come from other infections, such as Pasteurella bacteria or the parasite Encephalitozoon cuniculi. Keep the rabbit in a small, well-padded space so it does not fall and hurt itself, help it reach food and water, and call the vet quickly.

faqs.q: Will my rabbits get ear mites again after treatment?
faqs.a: They can, if mites are brought back in or survive in the hutch. To lower the risk, clean and sun-dry hutches and nest boxes, change bedding, quarantine new rabbits for a few weeks, check ears every week, and avoid overcrowding. Rabbits do not become fully immune, so good routine management is the best long-term protection.
