ear-mites.seoDescription: Ear mites (ear canker) in rabbits: spot head shaking and brown ear crusts early, act before the vet comes, and prevent Psoroptes spreading in your hutches.

card.headline: Bald, red or open sores on heels
card.look: The underside of the back feet, where the rabbit rests its weight, loses fur and turns pink or red. Later it becomes a scabbed or open sore, and the rabbit sits awkwardly or does not want to move.
card.action: Move the rabbit at once onto a clean, dry, soft resting surface such as a wooden board covered with dry hay, and check every other rabbit's feet.

detail.summary: Sore hocks are pressure sores on the underside of a rabbit's feet, mostly the back feet, where the rabbit rests its weight. They start as hair loss and red skin and can become deep infected wounds that reach tendons and bone. They are very common in rabbits kept on bare wire floors or wet, dirty bedding. They are painful and reduce growth, breeding and the value of your stock, but in most cases they can be prevented with good housing.
detail.cause: Rabbits have no foot pads like cats or dogs. Instead, a thick layer of fur on the underside of the foot acts as a cushion. When a rabbit sits for long hours on a hard, thin or uneven surface such as wire mesh, the pressure squeezes the skin between the floor and the small bones of the foot. Blood cannot flow well to that skin, so the fur wears away and the skin becomes thin, red and inflamed. Wet floors soaked with urine and droppings soften the skin and burn it with ammonia, making the damage faster. Heavy or overweight rabbits press harder on the same small area. Once the skin cracks, bacteria from the floor and the rabbit's own skin get in. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common germ involved, but others can join. The infection forms pus and abscesses (pockets of pus under the skin). If it is not stopped, it spreads deeper to the tendons (the cords that move the toes) and the bones, a condition called osteomyelitis (bone infection). At that stage the foot may stay damaged for life and the infection can spread through the blood.
spread: Sore hocks are not mainly a contagious disease; they are caused by poor floors and management, so many rabbits in the same unit often get them at the same time.
Bare wire mesh floors, especially thin wire, wide gaps or rusted and sagging mesh, put constant pressure on a small part of the foot.
Wet bedding and floors soaked with urine soften the skin and burn it with ammonia, so it breaks more easily.
Overweight rabbits and large heavy breeds press harder on their heels and wear the fur away faster.
Small cages where the rabbit cannot move around keep the weight on the same spot for most of the day.
Rabbits that stamp their feet a lot because of stress, noise, dogs or predators near the hutch damage their heels more quickly.
Long, overgrown nails push the weight back onto the heel instead of the toes, increasing pressure on the sore area.
Once a sore is open, bacteria from dirty floors, pus from other infected rabbits and dirty hands or tools can make the infection worse.
detail.atRisk: Any rabbit can get sore hocks, but some are more at risk. Heavy breeds such as Flemish Giant, New Zealand White and Californian, and rabbits that are overweight, carry more weight on their feet. Rex rabbits are especially prone because their short, thin fur gives little cushion on the feet. Adult breeding bucks and does are affected more than young growers because they stay in cages for many months or years, and older rabbits with stiff joints sit still more. Rabbits in raised hutches with bare wire floors, which are common in Kenyan backyard and commercial units, are at the highest risk, as are rabbits on floors that are rarely cleaned. The problem often gets worse in the long and short rains, when hutches stay damp and bedding does not dry. Rabbits that cannot move much because of small cages, arthritis or other illness also develop sores faster.

early: Thinning fur or a small bald patch on the underside of the back feet, usually at the heel area that touches the floor when the rabbit sits.
Pink or red skin in the bald patch, sometimes dry, flaky or slightly thickened like a callus.
The rabbit shifts its weight from foot to foot, or sits leaning forward onto its front feet to take weight off its heels.
The rabbit moves less around the cage, lies stretched out more than usual, or hesitates to hop.
Fur on the feet looks stained yellow or brown from urine and is damp or matted.
The rabbit flinches or pulls the foot away when you gently touch the sole.
advanced: Open sores or ulcers on the heel, often covered with a dark scab that may crack and bleed a little.
Swelling of the foot or heel, and thick yellow or white pus under a scab or coming out of the sore.
A bad smell from the feet, especially when infection is deep.
Clear lameness, refusing to stand on the foot, or the rabbit sitting hunched in one corner.
Reduced appetite, weight loss and a rough, poor coat because of pain and infection.
The toes look twisted or the foot sits at an odd angle, which can mean the tendon has slipped or the bone is infected.
Breeding bucks refuse to mount does, and does lose condition or neglect their litters.
In very severe cases the rabbit becomes weak and dull because infection has spread through the body.

lookalikes.name: Ringworm (fungal skin infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ringworm gives round, scaly, bald patches mainly on the head, ears, nose and around the paws, not only on the weight-bearing heel. It does not usually form deep pus-filled sores. It can spread to people, so a vet should check any scaly bald patches.

lookalikes.name: Mange mites (Sarcoptes or Notoedres)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange causes thick, grey-white crusts on the nose, lips, ears and toes, and the rabbit scratches and shakes intensely. Sore hocks are on the underside of the heel, are painful rather than itchy, and match where the rabbit sits on the floor.

lookalikes.name: Urine scald
lookalikes.howToTell: Urine scald causes red, sore, wet skin around the genitals, belly and inner back legs from sitting in urine. It often happens together with sore hocks in dirty hutches, but the main damage is higher up the legs, not on the heel itself.

lookalikes.name: Leg injury, fracture or splay leg
lookalikes.howToTell: A broken leg or dislocation gives sudden severe lameness, often after a fall or rough handling, and the leg may hang or move abnormally. Splay leg is seen in young kits whose legs stick out sideways. The heels look normal unless sore hocks are also present.

detail.diagnosis: Most cases are diagnosed by a vet or animal health assistant simply by looking at and feeling the feet. They usually grade how bad it is, from mild hair loss and red skin to deep infection with bone involvement, because this guides treatment and the decision to treat or cull. If there is pus, the vet may take a swab for culture and sensitivity, a lab test that finds which bacteria are present and which antibiotics will work. If the foot is swollen or deformed, an X-ray may be suggested to check whether the bone is infected; this is not always available on farm, so the vet may judge from the look and feel of the foot. The vet will also check the rabbit's weight, teeth, nails and general health, because overweight rabbits, overgrown nails and arthritis all make sore hocks worse. To help, the farmer should record when the problem was first noticed, how many rabbits are affected, the type of floor and bedding, how often the hutch is cleaned, the diet, and any treatment already tried. Clear photos of the feet and of the cage floor are very useful.
firstSteps: Move the affected rabbit straight away onto a clean, dry, soft surface, such as a smooth wooden board or solid plastic floor covered with plenty of dry hay, straw or wood shavings.
Gently look at both back feet and both front feet, then check every other rabbit in the unit, because rabbits housed the same way often have the same problem.
If the feet are dirty, wipe them gently with clean, lukewarm boiled water and pat them dry with a clean cloth; do not soak the rabbit or leave the fur wet.
Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap before and after touching sores, and keep rabbits with pus-filled sores in a separate clean cage.
Put feed, hay and water where the rabbit can reach them without hopping far, and make sure it keeps eating, because rabbits that stop eating can become seriously ill quickly.
Do not apply human creams, used engine oil, paraffin, salt or other home remedies, and do not wrap the foot tightly yourself, as tight bandages can cut off blood flow.
Do not give any antibiotic or medicine without a vet, because several common antibiotics can kill rabbits by upsetting their gut.
Write down which rabbits are affected and how bad each foot looks, and call your vet or animal health assistant if there is an open sore, pus, swelling, lameness or poor appetite.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how severe the sores are, and every treatment must be prescribed by a vet. In mild cases, where there is only hair loss and redness, the main treatment is fixing the housing: soft, dry, clean flooring, weight control and nail trimming. The vet may show you how to clean the feet with a mild antiseptic and apply a soothing dressing. For open or infected sores, the vet will clip the fur, clean the wound, remove dead tissue and pus, and may apply a padded dressing or bandage that must be checked and changed regularly. Pain relief is important because sore hocks hurt; vets commonly use anti-inflammatory painkillers such as meloxicam. If infection is deep, the vet may prescribe antibiotics, ideally chosen after a culture and sensitivity test. Rabbits are very sensitive to some antibiotics: penicillins and amoxicillin given by mouth, and lincomycin or clindamycin, can destroy the good gut bacteria and cause fatal diarrhoea, which is why you must never treat rabbits with antibiotics bought for other animals. Vets often choose rabbit-safe options such as enrofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfonamide combinations. Use antibiotics only when prescribed, complete the full course, and do not use them to cover up bad housing, because misuse breeds antimicrobial resistance (germs that drugs no longer kill). If you keep rabbits for meat, ask your vet about the withdrawal period, the time you must wait after the last treatment before slaughter, and follow it strictly. Severe cases with bone infection or a slipped tendon may need surgery, long treatment over many weeks, or humane culling if the rabbit cannot be kept free of pain. Healing is slow, often taking weeks, and sores return if the floor is not changed.
prevention: Give every rabbit a solid resting area covering part of the cage floor, such as a smooth untreated wooden board, plastic slatted panel or rubber mat, so it can take its weight off the wire.
If you use wire floors, choose strong, flat, smooth mesh that does not sag, replace rusted or broken wire, and never keep heavy breeds on thin wire with wide gaps.
Keep floors dry: clean droppings and wet bedding daily, make sure urine drains away from the rabbit, and replace bedding more often during the long and short rains.
Provide dry, clean bedding such as hay, straw or wood shavings, and avoid hard, rough or sharp materials on the floor.
Control body weight by feeding plenty of good hay and fresh greens and limiting pellets, maize bran and other energy-rich feeds, especially for adult breeding stock.
Give rabbits enough space to move, stretch and hop, and where possible let them exercise on grass or soft ground in a safe run.
Check the underside of each rabbit's feet at least once a week, and act as soon as you see thinning fur or pink skin.
Trim overgrown nails regularly, keep the hutch away from dogs, noise and predators that cause stamping, and avoid breeding from rabbits with thin foot fur or repeated sore hocks.
detail.impact: Sore hocks are rarely a sudden killer, but they quietly cost Kenyan rabbit farmers money. Painful rabbits eat less, so growers take longer to reach market weight and meat rabbits lose value. Breeding bucks with sore feet often refuse to mate, and does in pain may lose condition, produce fewer or weaker litters, or neglect their kits, which reduces the number of rabbits you can sell. Severe cases need vet visits, dressings and medicines, and some valuable breeding animals end up culled early. Damaged fur and scarred feet also lower the value of pelts and of breeding stock sold to other farmers. Because the same housing affects all rabbits, one neglected unit can see many animals affected at once, and poor animal welfare can harm a farm's reputation with buyers.
detail.humanHealth: Sore hocks themselves do not spread to people, but infected sores often contain Staphylococcus aureus and other bacteria that can infect cuts on human hands. Wear gloves or wash your hands well with soap and water after handling sores, dressings and bedding, and cover any cuts on your hands. Burn or bury used dressings safely. If a rabbit has been treated with antibiotics, do not slaughter it for food until the withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed, to avoid drug residues in the meat.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good when sore hocks are caught early, at the stage of hair loss and red skin, and the housing is fixed straight away. Many of these rabbits recover fully, although the fur may grow back thin. Once there are open sores with infection, healing is slower and takes weeks of careful nursing and vet treatment, but many rabbits still improve. If the infection has reached the tendons or bone, the outlook is guarded to poor, and the foot may stay painful or deformed; culling may then be the kindest choice. Recovery is better in rabbits of healthy weight, with trimmed nails, on soft, dry floors. The biggest reason for failure is returning the rabbit to the same wire floor or wet hutch, because sores very often come back.

faqs.q: Do I have to stop using wire floors completely?
faqs.a: Not always, but bare wire on its own is a major cause of sore hocks. Many farmers keep wire floors so droppings fall through, but add a solid resting board or plastic mat over part of the floor so each rabbit can sit off the wire. Make sure the wire is strong, flat and smooth, and replace sagging or rusted mesh. Heavy breeds and Rex rabbits especially need more solid or bedded floor space.

faqs.q: Is sore hocks contagious to my other rabbits?
faqs.a: The sores themselves are caused by pressure and dampness, not by catching them from another rabbit. However, pus from infected sores contains bacteria that can infect other rabbits with broken skin, so keep rabbits with pus-filled sores separate and clean their cages carefully. If several rabbits have sore hocks at the same time, it is a sign that the housing or management needs changing for the whole unit.

faqs.q: Can I treat sore hocks with salt, paraffin or a cream from the shop?
faqs.a: It is best not to. Salt and paraffin can burn damaged skin, and some creams are toxic if rabbits lick them. Gently wiping the feet with clean, lukewarm boiled water and drying them, then moving the rabbit to a soft dry floor, is safe. For open or infected sores, ask your vet which antiseptic and dressing to use. Never give antibiotics without a vet, because some common ones can kill rabbits.

faqs.q: Why are my breeding bucks and big does affected more than the young rabbits?
faqs.a: Adult breeding rabbits stay in the same cage for months or years, are heavier, and often move less, so the same small part of the foot carries their weight day after day. Young growers are lighter and are usually sold before the damage builds up. Giving breeding stock solid resting areas, more space, exercise and careful weight control greatly reduces the problem.

faqs.q: Should I cull a rabbit with sore hocks?
faqs.a: Most rabbits with early sore hocks do not need culling; they recover when the housing is fixed. Culling may be the kindest and most practical choice if the infection has reached the bone, the foot is deformed, the rabbit remains in pain despite treatment, or it keeps getting sores again. Discuss this with your vet, and avoid breeding from rabbits that repeatedly develop sore hocks or have very thin fur on their feet.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell a rabbit that has sore hocks?
faqs.a: A rabbit with mild sores that is otherwise healthy and has not been given medicines can usually be slaughtered for food in the normal way. Do not slaughter a rabbit that is sick, weak, thin or has spreading infection, and ask your vet first. If the rabbit has had antibiotics or other drugs, wait until the full withdrawal period your vet gives you has passed before slaughter.

card.headline: No droppings, hunched rabbit, swollen belly
card.look: The rabbit sits hunched in a corner, refuses food and passes few or no droppings. Its belly may feel tight or swollen, it may grind its teeth, and young rabbits may pass clear, jelly-like mucus.
card.action: Treat this as an emergency: keep the rabbit warm and quiet, offer hay and water, and call a vet the same day, because rabbits with a stopped gut can die within a day or two.

aka: Sungura (Swahili for rabbit); farmers often describe a bloated belly as 'tumbo kujaa gesi'
detail.summary: Gut stasis means a rabbit's digestive system slows down or stops moving food along. Gas and fermenting food build up and cause bloat and severe pain. In young rabbits around weaning, a related condition called mucoid enteropathy causes a swollen belly and jelly-like mucus in place of normal droppings. All of these are emergencies. Rabbits cannot vomit, and a rabbit that stops eating and passing droppings can die quickly, so fast action and a vet visit matter more than anything else.
detail.cause: A rabbit's gut is built to run on large amounts of fibre, mainly from hay and grass. Long fibre keeps the gut muscles moving, and the caecum (a large pouch at the start of the large intestine) holds friendly bacteria that ferment food. When the diet is low in fibre, for example mostly pellets, bread, maize bran, kitchen scraps or sugary vegetables, or when the rabbit is stressed, in pain, dehydrated or suddenly given a new feed, the gut slows down. Food and hair dry out inside the stomach and intestines. The balance of bacteria in the caecum changes, and harmful bacteria such as some Clostridium species can multiply, make gas and release toxins. Gas stretches the gut, which is very painful, and pain itself slows the gut further, creating a vicious cycle. In severe cases the stretched gut loses blood supply, toxins enter the blood and the rabbit goes into shock. Mucoid enteropathy in weaners is less well understood. It appears to involve disturbed gut bacteria at weaning, a low-fibre or sudden change of diet, and stress. The infectious form, epizootic rabbit enteropathy (ERE), spreads between rabbits in a unit, and its exact cause is still being studied, although bacteria are strongly suspected. In these young rabbits the large intestine fills with thick mucus, the caecum becomes impacted (packed hard with dry content) or bloated, and the rabbit stops eating and drinking. Underlying problems such as overgrown teeth, coccidiosis, a swallowed blockage or any painful illness can also trigger stasis, so it is often a sign of something else as well as a disease in its own right.
spread: Low-fibre feeding is the most common trigger: rations based mainly on pellets, grains, maize bran, bread, chapati or kitchen waste, with little hay or grass.
A sudden change of feed, such as switching pellet brands overnight or giving a large amount of fresh, wet or young lush greens to rabbits not used to them, upsets the gut bacteria.
Weaning stress in young rabbits, including separation from the doe, a new cage, mixing litters and a diet change all at once, is a major trigger for mucoid enteropathy.
The infectious form (ERE) spreads in rabbitries through droppings, contaminated cages, feeders, drinkers and the hands, boots and clothes of people moving between hutches.
Not drinking enough, because water is dirty, warm, frozen in nipple lines, or the drinker is blocked or empty, lets gut contents dry out.
Stress from heat, transport, dogs or predators near the hutch, loud noise, overcrowding or handling can make the gut slow down.
Pain from overgrown or sharp teeth, injuries, urinary problems or other diseases makes a rabbit stop eating, which then leads to stasis.
Mouldy or spoiled feed, eating hair when grooming during a moult, and swallowing carpet, cloth or sacking can contribute to slow gut and blockages.
detail.atRisk: Weaners and growers, roughly from weaning up to about three months of age, are most at risk of mucoid enteropathy and ERE, especially in larger commercial units where many young rabbits are kept together. Adult rabbits of any breed can develop gut stasis, especially those fed mostly pellets or kitchen scraps, older rabbits with dental problems, does after kindling and rabbits recovering from other illness or surgery. Long-haired breeds such as Angora are more likely to swallow hair. In Kenya, risk often rises during the long and short rains when grass is wet and lush and hay may be scarce or mouldy, and during hot dry spells when water runs low and heat stress is common. Backyard hutches fed on sukuma wiki, cabbage and leftovers with little dry roughage, and commercial units that push pellets for fast growth, are both at risk.

early: The rabbit eats less, picks only at favourite treats, or ignores pellets and hay altogether.
Droppings become smaller, fewer, drier or misshapen, or there are no fresh droppings under the cage in the morning.
The rabbit sits hunched and still in a corner, with half-closed eyes and less interest in its surroundings.
Soft, quiet teeth grinding can be heard, which in rabbits is usually a sign of pain.
The rabbit drinks less and its caecotrophs (the soft, shiny night droppings it normally eats) may be left smeared on the floor or fur.
Gurgling gut sounds may be louder than normal at first, or the belly may be unusually quiet.
advanced: No droppings at all for many hours, or only thin strings of jelly-like clear or whitish mucus coming from the vent.
The belly is swollen, tight or drum-like, and may slosh or feel doughy when gently touched.
Loud teeth grinding, pressing the belly against the floor, stretching out, or lying flat on one side because of severe pain.
Cold ears and feet, weakness, and reluctance or inability to stand, which suggest shock and low body temperature.
Dull, sunken eyes and skin that stays tented when gently pinched, showing dehydration.
In weaners with mucoid enteropathy, several young rabbits in the same pen become dull, bloated and stop eating within a few days, and some may die suddenly.

lookalikes.name: Intestinal coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis is caused by tiny parasites and is common in young rabbits on dirty floors. It usually causes watery or pasty diarrhoea, often with soiled back legs, weight loss and a pot belly over several days, rather than a sudden stop in droppings with jelly-like mucus. A vet can confirm it by finding coccidia eggs in a dung sample or gut lesions at post-mortem. The two problems can occur together.

lookalikes.name: Enterotoxaemia (Clostridium spiroforme)
lookalikes.howToTell: This is a sudden, severe bacterial toxin disease, often after weaning, a diet change or the wrong antibiotic. Rabbits usually have brown, watery, sometimes bloody or foul-smelling diarrhoea and may die within hours to a day or two. Mucoid enteropathy and simple stasis show few or no droppings and mucus instead of watery diarrhoea. Only a vet and post-mortem can reliably separate them.

lookalikes.name: Dental disease (overgrown teeth)
lookalikes.howToTell: Rabbits with tooth problems may drool, have a wet chin, drop food from the mouth, pick at soft food only or lose weight slowly over weeks. They can develop stasis because they stop eating, so a vet should check the teeth in any rabbit with gut slowdown.

lookalikes.name: Intestinal blockage (obstruction)
lookalikes.howToTell: A true blockage from a hair mat, swallowed fabric or a dried food plug often causes a very sudden onset, a rapidly swelling and very painful belly, and quick collapse. It can look like severe bloat, but it needs different treatment, so the vet will often use X-rays or careful examination to decide. Never force-feed a rabbit with a hard, swollen belly until a vet has ruled out a blockage.

detail.diagnosis: A vet starts by asking about the diet, recent feed changes, weaning, water supply and how long the rabbit has gone without eating or passing droppings. They will check body temperature, because a low temperature is a warning sign of shock, listen to the gut for sounds, gently feel the belly for gas, fluid or a hard impacted caecum, and examine the mouth and teeth. In clinics with equipment, X-rays help show whether there is gas spread through the gut or a single blockage, and blood tests can show dehydration and blood sugar levels, which help predict how serious the case is. A dung sample can be checked for coccidia. In a rabbitry where several weaners have died, a post-mortem on a fresh carcass is very valuable, because it shows mucus-filled intestines, an impacted caecum or signs of other diseases, and samples can be sent to a laboratory such as a county or national veterinary laboratory. To help the vet, note when the rabbit last ate and passed droppings, what it has been fed over the past two weeks, its age and whether others are affected, and keep any recent droppings or mucus in a clean bag. If a rabbit dies, keep the body cool, not frozen, in a sealed bag and contact the vet quickly.
firstSteps: Check the rabbit carefully now: look under the cage for fresh droppings, see whether it is eating, and gently feel whether the belly is soft or tight and swollen.
Call a vet or your County Veterinary Office the same day, and explain that the rabbit has stopped eating or passing droppings, because waiting even a day can be fatal.
Keep the rabbit warm and quiet in a draught-free, shaded spot, and if its ears feel cold, give it a towel-wrapped bottle of warm (not hot) water to lie near.
Offer plenty of good-quality, dry hay or fresh grass and clean, fresh water in both a bowl and a bottle, plus a few washed leafy greens to encourage eating and drinking.
Stop all pellets, bread, grains, sugary treats and kitchen scraps until the vet has seen the rabbit, and do not give home remedies such as cooking oil, salt water or human medicines.
Do not force-feed, massage hard or press on a tight, swollen belly, because a blocked or overstretched gut can be damaged; only gentle handling until the vet advises.
If several weaners are affected, move sick rabbits to a separate clean cage, clean feeders and drinkers, and attend to healthy rabbits before sick ones.
Wash your hands and change or clean footwear after handling sick rabbits, and write down each rabbit's age, feed, signs, when they started and any deaths.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on whether the gut has simply slowed down, is bloated with gas, or is blocked, so a vet must examine the rabbit and prescribe everything. The main aims are to relieve pain, correct dehydration, get the gut moving again and support the rabbit's energy. Vets commonly give fluids by injection under the skin or into a vein, pain relief such as meloxicam (an anti-inflammatory) or buprenorphine (a stronger painkiller), and sometimes medicines that help the gut move, such as metoclopramide, once a blockage has been ruled out. Simethicone may be used to help break up gas, and the rabbit is kept warm. When it is safe, the vet may advise syringe feeding with a fibre-rich recovery food, and will show you how to do it. Antibiotics are not routine for simple stasis. They are used only when the vet suspects a bacterial problem, such as in ERE outbreaks or enterotoxaemia, and the choice matters greatly: some antibiotics given by mouth, including many penicillins, amoxicillin, lincomycin and clindamycin, can upset rabbit gut bacteria and cause fatal diarrhoea. Only use antibiotics a vet prescribes for rabbits, complete the course as directed and never share or reuse leftover drugs, because misuse drives antimicrobial resistance, which makes future infections harder to treat in animals and people. For outbreaks in commercial units, a vet may recommend medicated feed or water for a group alongside diet changes. Any rabbit treated with drugs and kept for meat must not be slaughtered for food until the withdrawal period on the label or set by the vet has passed. True blockages may need surgery, which carries real risk in rabbits. Expect daily checks on eating and droppings; improvement is usually seen within one to three days if treatment works.
prevention: Make hay or dry grass the main part of the diet, available at all times, with pellets given in limited amounts rather than unlimited, because long fibre keeps the gut moving.
Change feeds slowly over one to two weeks, mixing old and new pellets, and introduce fresh greens gradually in small amounts, especially lush, wet grass in the rains.
Wean young rabbits gently: avoid changing the cage, the diet and the group all at once, keep weaners with litter-mates, and give plenty of hay during and after weaning.
Provide clean, fresh water at all times, check nipple drinkers daily for blockages, and add extra drinkers and shade during hot weather.
Store hay and pellets dry and off the floor, and throw away any feed that is mouldy, dusty, damp or smells bad.
Keep cages clean and dry, remove droppings regularly, and clean and disinfect cages, feeders and drinkers between batches of weaners to reduce ERE and coccidiosis.
Reduce stress by avoiding overcrowding, keeping dogs and predators away, handling rabbits calmly and providing shade and ventilation in hot spells.
Check teeth, droppings and appetite daily, groom long-haired rabbits during moults, and quarantine new rabbits for at least two to three weeks before mixing them with the herd.
detail.impact: Gut stasis and mucoid enteropathy are among the most important causes of death in growing rabbits, and losses can be heavy in commercial units when ERE moves through a batch of weaners. Rabbits that survive often grow slowly, reach market weight late and use more feed for each kilo gained, which cuts into thin margins. In breeding does, illness can lead to poor milk, weak litters or lost pregnancies. Vet fees, medicines and the time spent nursing sick rabbits add costs, and meat rabbits under treatment cannot be sold until withdrawal periods end. For Kenyan smallholders who sell rabbits to hotels, butcheries or other breeders, repeated losses can damage reputation and contracts. The good news is that most prevention, such as more hay, slow feed changes, clean water and calm weaning, is cheap compared with the cost of lost rabbits.
detail.humanHealth: Gut stasis and mucoid enteropathy are not known to spread to people. However, sick rabbits may carry bacteria in their droppings, so wash your hands with soap after handling them or cleaning cages, and keep children from handling sick animals. If a vet treats rabbits kept for meat, follow the meat withdrawal period strictly so that drug residues do not end up in food, and do not eat rabbits that died of illness.
detail.outlook: Outlook depends mostly on how quickly treatment starts and how sick the rabbit is when seen. Adult rabbits with mild stasis caught early, while they still have some appetite, normal body temperature and soft belly, often recover well with vet care and a high-fibre diet. Rabbits with a hard, bloated belly, low body temperature, collapse or a true blockage have a much poorer outlook, and some die despite treatment. Mucoid enteropathy and ERE in weaners carry a guarded outlook, and deaths in an affected batch are common, so prevention is far more reliable than cure. Rabbits that have had stasis once can get it again, especially if the diet or underlying cause, such as dental disease, is not corrected.

faqs.q: How long can a rabbit go without passing droppings before I should worry?
faqs.a: A healthy rabbit produces droppings almost constantly through the day and night. If you see no fresh droppings for around 8 to 12 hours, or the rabbit has stopped eating, treat it as urgent and call a vet. Do not wait until the next day to see if it improves on its own, because rabbits can go downhill very fast.

faqs.q: Can I give my rabbit cooking oil or liquid paraffin to clear the gut?
faqs.a: No. Oils do not fix the underlying problem, can be breathed into the lungs and may make things worse, and they can hide a blockage that needs proper vet care. Offer hay, water and fresh greens, keep the rabbit warm, and let the vet decide which treatment is safe.

faqs.q: Why are my weaners dying with swollen bellies and jelly in their droppings?
faqs.a: This pattern is typical of mucoid enteropathy or the infectious form called epizootic rabbit enteropathy, which strikes rabbits around weaning. Low-fibre feeding, sudden diet changes, stress at weaning and spread between rabbits all play a part. Call a vet quickly, separate sick rabbits, clean cages and equipment, increase hay for the whole group and ask the vet about a post-mortem on a fresh carcass so the cause can be confirmed.

faqs.q: Are pellets bad for rabbits?
faqs.a: Pellets are not bad, and good-quality pellets supply useful protein, minerals and vitamins, especially for fast-growing meat rabbits. The problem comes when pellets replace hay and grass. Keep hay or dry grass available all the time, give pellets in measured amounts, and make any change of pellet brand slowly over one to two weeks.

faqs.q: Can I give my rabbit an antibiotic from the agrovet to be safe?
faqs.a: Please do not. Many common antibiotics, especially some given by mouth, can kill the helpful bacteria in a rabbit's gut and cause deadly diarrhoea. Simple gut stasis often does not need antibiotics at all. Only use antibiotics that a vet has prescribed specifically for rabbits, follow the instructions exactly and respect the meat withdrawal period.

faqs.q: Is sukuma wiki or cabbage safe for rabbits?
faqs.a: Small amounts of washed, fresh leafy greens can be part of a rabbit's diet, but they should not be the main feed, and large amounts of cabbage or wet, freshly cut greens given suddenly can upset the gut and cause gas. Build the diet on hay or dry grass, introduce greens gradually, and avoid wilted, mouldy or spoiled vegetables and leftovers.
