gut-stasis.seoDescription: Rabbit gut stasis and bloat: spot no droppings, hunched posture and teeth grinding early, act fast, and prevent it with high-fibre hay and calm weaning.

card.headline: Hot, swollen red or blue teats
card.look: One or more teats and the surrounding breast tissue on a nursing doe are swollen, hard, hot and red, sometimes turning dark blue or purple. The doe sits hunched, refuses feed and will not let her kits nurse, so the kits look thin, wrinkled and cry in the nest.
card.action: Separate the sick doe and her kits into a clean, quiet hutch, wash your hands, and call a vet the same day because rabbit mastitis can kill a doe within one or two days.

detail.summary: Mastitis is a bacterial infection of the mammary glands (breasts) of a doe, usually in the first few weeks after kindling (giving birth). The breasts become hot, swollen and painful, the doe gets a fever and stops eating, and her milk dries up or becomes infected. It matters because a doe can die quickly from blood poisoning, her kits can starve or catch the infection, and the bacteria can spread through a rabbitry on hands, bedding and fostered kits.
detail.cause: Mastitis is caused by bacteria getting into the teat or breast tissue. The most common culprit is Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium that lives on skin and in the environment; some strains are very aggressive and cause the severe 'blue breast' form. Pasteurella multocida, Streptococcus species, E. coli and Klebsiella are also found. Bacteria usually enter through small wounds on the teats made by the kits' sharp teeth, scratches from wire floors or rough nest boxes, or through dirty, wet bedding. Milk building up in the glands also helps infection take hold, which happens when a doe has more milk than her kits drink, when a litter dies, or when kits are weaned suddenly. Once inside, the bacteria multiply in the warm, milk-filled tissue. The body sends blood and fluid to fight them, causing heat, redness and swelling. In severe cases bacterial toxins kill the tissue and cut off its blood supply, so the skin turns blue or black (gangrene, meaning dead tissue). Toxins and bacteria can then enter the bloodstream (septicaemia, or blood poisoning), which causes high fever, collapse and death.
spread: Kits suckling on an infected doe can carry bacteria in their mouths and on their faces, so fostering those kits onto a healthy doe can spread mastitis to her.
Farmers' hands carry bacteria from one doe to the next when checking nests or handling litters without washing in between.
Dirty, damp or soiled nest material and bedding hold large numbers of bacteria that enter small cuts on the teats.
Sharp wire, broken hutch floors, rough nest-box edges and splinters scratch the teats and let bacteria in.
Kits with sharp teeth, especially large litters fighting for too few teats, nick and bruise the teats.
Milk build-up after a litter dies, after sudden weaning, or when a doe has a very small litter makes the glands an easy target for infection.
Shared equipment such as nest boxes and feeders that are not cleaned between litters keep the bacteria in the rabbitry.
detail.atRisk: Nursing does in the first three weeks after kindling are most at risk, and again around weaning when milk builds up. Heavy-milking meat breeds commonly kept in Kenya, such as New Zealand White, California and Flemish Giant crosses, are often affected. Does with very small litters or whose litters have died, does on wire floors without a resting board, and does kept in crowded, damp or poorly cleaned hutches face higher risk. The long and short rains bring wet bedding and damp hutches, which raises bacterial loads. Rabbitries that foster kits freely between does, or that bring in new stock without quarantine, can see repeated cases. Older does that have had mastitis before, and unspayed older does with breast changes, may also have problems.

early: One or more teats look pink to red and feel warmer than the others when you gently touch the belly.
The breast tissue around a teat feels firm, lumpy or swollen instead of soft.
The doe flinches, grunts or moves away when touched on the belly, and may stop sitting over the nest to feed her kits.
She eats less than usual, leaves pellets or greens uneaten and drinks less.
The kits look less full: bellies are flat rather than round and white with milk, and they may cry or crawl about the nest.
The doe may sit hunched and quiet in a corner more than normal.
advanced: Teats and breasts turn dark red, purple, blue or black and may feel cold in the centre where tissue is dying.
The swelling becomes large, hard and very hot, and may spread across several glands.
Pus or thick, discoloured, bloody or watery fluid may come from the teat, or an abscess (pus-filled lump) forms and bursts.
The doe stops eating and drinking completely, her droppings become small or stop, and she breathes fast.
She becomes very weak, lies flat, feels hot to touch or later cold as she goes into shock.
Kits become thin, wrinkled, dehydrated and weak, and some die in the nest; surviving kits may develop skin abscesses or infections themselves.
Sudden death of the doe can happen within one to two days in the severe blue-breast form.

lookalikes.name: Caked breasts (milk stasis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Milk simply builds up when kits die, are weaned suddenly or the litter is small. The glands are full and firm but usually not very hot, red or blue, and the doe keeps eating and has no fever. Caked breasts can turn into mastitis if not managed, so watch closely and ask a vet if in doubt.

lookalikes.name: Abscess on the belly or chest
lookalikes.howToTell: An abscess is a single, round, well-defined lump of pus, often caused by Pasteurella, and it can appear at any time, not just after kindling. Mastitis involves the milk glands themselves, starts around the teats and usually makes a nursing doe sick quickly.

lookalikes.name: Mammary tumours or cystic breasts
lookalikes.howToTell: These are seen mostly in older does that are not used for breeding or have had many litters. Lumps grow slowly over weeks or months, are usually not hot or painful, and the doe stays bright and eating.

lookalikes.name: Moist dermatitis (sore, wet skin)
lookalikes.howToTell: Skin on the belly, dewlap or between the legs is wet, red and smelly from urine, drooling or damp bedding, but the breast tissue under it is soft and not swollen. The doe is usually not feverish.

detail.diagnosis: A vet diagnoses mastitis mainly by examining the doe: looking at and feeling each mammary gland, checking colour, heat, swelling and any discharge, and taking her temperature, because a fever supports infection. The vet will also check her hydration, gut sounds and droppings, since a doe that stops eating can develop gut stasis (the gut slowing or stopping), and will examine the kits. Where there are repeated cases on a farm, the vet may take a sample of milk or pus to a laboratory for culture, which identifies the bacteria, and a sensitivity test, which shows which antibiotics will work. This is very useful in Kenya where some bacteria are resistant to common drugs. If a doe dies, a post-mortem by a vet or county veterinary laboratory can confirm the cause and protect the rest of the herd. Before the vet arrives, write down when the doe kindled, litter size, when you first saw signs, what she has eaten, any kits that died, and whether any kits were fostered. Keep the doe in a clean box so the vet can see the glands clearly, and do not apply creams or home remedies that hide the signs.
firstSteps: Move the sick doe and her kits into a clean, dry, quiet hutch away from other nursing does, ideally with a solid resting board over any wire floor.
Do not foster her kits onto another doe without a vet's advice, because the kits can carry the bacteria and give mastitis to a healthy doe.
Wash your hands with soap and water before and after touching her, wear disposable gloves if you have them, and handle her last after all healthy rabbits.
Offer fresh clean water in a bowl as well as the drinker, plus her favourite fresh greens such as clean sukuma wiki leaves, grasses or hay, to tempt her to keep eating.
Check the kits several times a day: note whether their bellies are full, whether they are warm, and how many are alive, and keep the nest clean, dry and warm.
Replace soiled nest material with clean, dry hay or wood shavings and remove anything sharp or rough in the hutch that could scratch her teats.
Do not try to squeeze out a hard, blue or black gland or cut into a lump, as this can push infection into the blood and is very painful.
Record her temperature if you have a thermometer and are confident using it, along with appetite and droppings, then call your vet or the County Veterinary Office the same day.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment must be prescribed by a vet, and rabbits need special care because many common antibiotics are dangerous to them. Some drugs, especially penicillins and related drugs given by mouth, lincomycin and clindamycin, can upset the rabbit's gut bacteria and cause fatal diarrhoea. A vet will choose an antibiotic that is safer for rabbits and suits the likely bacteria; drug groups often used include fluoroquinolones such as enrofloxacin, potentiated sulphonamides such as trimethoprim-sulfa, and in some cases carefully chosen injectable antibiotics. Where possible a culture and sensitivity test guides the choice. The vet will usually give a pain-relieving anti-inflammatory drug, because pain stops the doe eating, and may give fluids if she is dehydrated. Warm compresses may be advised for early, hard glands. Abscesses may need to be lanced and flushed, and in the severe gangrenous form dead tissue may have to be surgically removed, which is not always possible. The vet will also advise on the kits: whether they can keep nursing, need hand-feeding, or can be fostered safely, and young kits that lose their mother's milk are hard to raise. Complete the full course of any antibiotic exactly as prescribed, never share leftover drugs with other rabbits, and respect the meat withdrawal period the vet gives before any treated rabbit is slaughtered. Using the wrong antibiotic, stopping early or treating without a vet helps create antimicrobial resistance, meaning bacteria that drugs can no longer kill, which harms animals and people. Expect improvement in early cases within a few days; severe cases may not survive even with good treatment.
prevention: Keep hutches and nest boxes clean and dry, change nest bedding when it is soiled or damp, and clean and disinfect nest boxes between litters.
Remove sharp wire ends, splinters and rough edges, and give does a solid resting board or mat so their teats do not rub on wire floors.
Wash hands between handling different does and litters, and check healthy does before any sick one.
Check the doe's belly gently every day or two in the first three weeks after kindling so you catch redness or firmness early.
Balance litter size: avoid leaving a high-milking doe with only one or two kits, and when fostering is needed, only foster healthy kits between healthy does of similar kindling dates.
Wean gradually over several days rather than removing all kits at once, and reduce concentrate feeding slightly around weaning to help milk production slow down.
Never foster kits from a doe with mastitis onto another doe, and cull or stop breeding does that suffer repeated or severe mastitis, as they often relapse and spread bacteria.
Quarantine new rabbits for about three to four weeks before mixing them in, and feed a balanced ration with good hay, clean greens and fresh water to keep does strong through lactation.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan smallholder or commercial rabbit farm, mastitis can wipe out a whole litter of six to ten kits through starvation, and a valuable breeding doe may die or have to be culled. Each lost litter means lost meat sales and lost replacement stock, and a doe that recovers may produce less milk in the affected glands next time. Vet visits, drugs and the time spent hand-feeding kits add cost. When the aggressive staphylococcal form gets into a rabbitry, it can cause repeated cases across many does, forcing farmers to cull breeding stock and clean out the whole unit, which sets production back by months. Rabbits treated with antibiotics cannot be sold for meat until the withdrawal period is over.
detail.humanHealth: Staphylococcus aureus and Pasteurella, the bacteria that most often cause rabbit mastitis, can also infect people, usually through cuts, scratches or bites, causing skin infections or painful, swollen wounds. Some Staphylococcus strains are resistant to antibiotics. Wear gloves or wash hands well with soap and water after handling a sick doe, her kits or her bedding, cover any cuts on your hands, and clean scratches promptly. Do not eat rabbits that died of mastitis or slaughter a sick doe for food. Respect the meat withdrawal period given by the vet after any antibiotic treatment so that drug residues do not reach your family or customers. People with weak immune systems, young children and the elderly should avoid handling infected rabbits, and anyone with a red, hot or spreading wound should see a health worker.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends mostly on how early treatment starts and which bacteria are involved. Does with early, red, firm glands that are treated promptly by a vet often recover, though the affected gland may produce less milk afterwards. Does with blue or black, cold glands, high fever or collapse have a poor outlook and many die despite treatment. A doe that stops eating can also develop gut stasis, which worsens her chances. Kits under about two to three weeks old are at serious risk because they depend fully on milk; older kits that are already eating solid food survive better. Does that recover may get mastitis again in later litters, and repeated cases are a sign to retire her from breeding and review hygiene in the whole rabbitry.

faqs.q: Can the kits keep suckling from a doe with mastitis?
faqs.a: It depends on how bad it is, so ask your vet. In mild cases the vet may allow kits to keep nursing from the healthy glands. In severe cases the milk may be infected, the doe may refuse to nurse, and kits can catch skin or other infections, so they may need to be removed. Do not foster them onto another doe without advice, because they can carry the bacteria and start mastitis in her.

faqs.q: Why can't I just give my rabbit the same antibiotic I use for my cows or goats?
faqs.a: Rabbits have a delicate gut full of helpful bacteria. Several antibiotics that are safe in cattle or goats, especially some penicillins and related drugs given by mouth, can kill those helpful bacteria and cause severe, often fatal diarrhoea in rabbits. Doses also differ greatly. Only a vet should choose the drug, and using the wrong one also helps create antibiotic resistance.

faqs.q: My doe's breasts are hard but she is still eating. Is that mastitis?
faqs.a: It may be caked breasts, meaning milk build-up, especially if her litter is small, some kits died or you just weaned them. If the glands are not very hot, red or blue and she is eating and active, it may settle. But caked breasts can quickly become infected, so check her twice a day and call the vet if she goes off feed, the skin changes colour, or the glands get hotter.

faqs.q: Should I keep breeding a doe that has had mastitis?
faqs.a: A doe that had one mild case and recovered fully may breed again, but watch her closely after each kindling. Does that had the severe blue form, lost glands, or get mastitis again are often best retired from breeding, because they are likely to relapse and can carry bacteria that spread to other does.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell a doe that had mastitis?
faqs.a: Never eat a rabbit that died of mastitis or slaughter one that is visibly sick. If a doe recovers after treatment, she can only be used for meat after the full withdrawal period the vet gives for the drugs used has passed, so that no drug residues are left in the meat.

faqs.q: How do I stop mastitis coming back in my rabbitry?
faqs.a: Focus on cleanliness and comfort: dry, clean nest boxes, resting boards over wire floors, no sharp edges, handwashing between hutches, and daily belly checks after kindling. Wean gradually, avoid tiny litters on heavy-milking does, never foster kits from a sick doe, and retire does with repeated cases. If many does are affected, ask your vet to culture samples so the right drugs and cleaning plan can be used.

mastitis.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of the underside of a white New Zealand White doe rabbit lying in a straw-lined wooden hutch, showing one swollen, reddish-purple teat and surrounding breast tissue among normal pink teats, soft natural light, realistic and not graphic.
mastitis.seoDescription: Mastitis in rabbit does: spot hot, red or blue swollen teats after kindling, protect starving kits, act before the vet arrives and prevent repeat cases.

card.headline: Rabbit lying stretched out, panting fast
card.look: The rabbit lies flat on its side or belly with legs stretched out, breathing very fast. Its ears are red and hot, and its chin and nose may be wet with drool.
card.action: Move the rabbit at once to the coolest shaded place you have, wet its ears with cool (not ice-cold) water, offer drinking water and call the vet.

detail.summary: Heat stress happens when a rabbit's body gets hotter than it can cool down. Rabbits cannot sweat and pant poorly, so they handle hot weather badly, especially above about 30 °C or in humid, poorly ventilated hutches. Mild heat stress cuts feeding, growth and fertility. Severe heat stress, called heat stroke, can kill a rabbit within hours, so treat it as an emergency.
detail.cause: Rabbits are built for cool conditions. They have no useful sweat glands and a thick coat. Their main way to lose heat is through the large blood vessels in their ears, plus faster breathing. Rabbits feel most comfortable at roughly 15–21 °C. As the air around them warms towards 28–30 °C, especially when the air is humid or still, these cooling methods stop being enough. Body heat then builds up. The rabbit breathes faster and faster, loses water, and its blood thickens. If its body temperature keeps rising, the heat starts to damage the brain, heart, liver, kidneys and gut. This causes weakness, fits (convulsions), collapse and death. Even rabbits that survive can suffer gut slowdown (gut stasis, when the gut stops moving food along), and bucks may become temporarily infertile because heat damages sperm production.
spread: Heat stress is not infectious and does not spread from rabbit to rabbit. It is triggered by hot conditions and poor management.
Hot weather is the main trigger, especially in the hot dry months before the long and short rains and in hot lowland areas.
Hutches under bare iron sheet (mabati) roofs with no insulation or ceiling get very hot by midday.
Poor airflow, such as closed boxes, solid walls, or hutches crowded against a wall, traps heat and moisture.
Overcrowding raises the temperature inside each cage because every rabbit gives off body heat.
Running out of water, or water that is warm, dirty or hard to reach, quickly makes heat stress worse.
Carrying rabbits to market or between farms in sacks, closed boxes or car boots in the sun is a common cause of sudden deaths.
Handling, chasing, mating or weighing rabbits during the hottest hours of the day adds extra heat and stress.
detail.atRisk: Any rabbit can suffer heat stress, but some are at much higher risk. These include does in late pregnancy and nursing does, very fat rabbits, and young kits in nest boxes full of fur and bedding. Heavy and thick-coated breeds such as Flemish Giant, New Zealand White, Californian, Chinchilla and long-haired Angora suffer more than small, lean local rabbits. Breeding bucks are at risk of heat-related infertility. Old or sick rabbits, especially those with breathing problems, cope poorly. In Kenya, risk is highest in hot lowland areas such as the Coast, the Lake Basin, lower Eastern (Machakos, Makueni, Kitui) and North Eastern, and during heat waves anywhere, including the highlands. Rabbits kept in metal cages, under iron sheets, in small backyard hutches with no shade, or transported during the day are the most vulnerable.

early: Faster breathing than normal, with the nose and sides moving quickly.
Lying stretched out flat, often on the side or belly, trying to press against a cool floor.
Ears feel hot to the touch and look red or pink because blood is rushing to them to lose heat.
Less feeding, especially during the day, and drinking much more water than usual.
Dull, quiet behaviour and not wanting to move or be handled.
Damp fur around the mouth and chin from drooling or licking.
advanced: Breathing with the mouth open. Rabbits normally breathe only through the nose, so this is a very serious warning sign.
Wet chin, nose and front paws from heavy drooling.
Weakness, wobbling, falling over or being unable to stand.
Bluish tinge to the lips or inside of the ears in some cases.
Shaking, fits (convulsions) or twitching of the head and legs.
Not responding when touched, collapse and, without quick help, death.
In nursing does and kits, sudden deaths in the nest box on hot afternoons.

lookalikes.name: Snuffles (Pasteurella respiratory infection)
lookalikes.howToTell: Snuffles causes sneezing, thick white or yellow nose discharge and matted front paws. It lasts days or weeks and does not depend on the weather. Heat stress comes on during hot hours and usually improves quickly when the rabbit is cooled.

lookalikes.name: Dental disease (overgrown teeth, 'slobbers')
lookalikes.howToTell: Overgrown teeth also cause a wet chin, but the rabbit drops food, loses weight over weeks and may have lumps on the jaw. Breathing and ear temperature are normal. Heat stress gives a wet chin together with fast breathing and hot red ears on a hot day.

lookalikes.name: Gut stasis or bloat (enteritis)
lookalikes.howToTell: A rabbit with gut problems sits hunched, grinds its teeth, produces few or no droppings, or has diarrhoea, and the belly may be swollen or tight. Heat-stressed rabbits lie stretched out and breathe fast. Gut stasis can also follow heat stress, so both may occur together.

lookalikes.name: Poisoning or nervous disease (such as Encephalitozoon, which causes head tilt)
lookalikes.howToTell: Poisoning or nervous disease can cause fits, but they occur regardless of temperature. There may be a history of new plants, sprayed feed or rat poison, or a slow-developing head tilt. Heat-related fits happen during hot weather together with very fast breathing and hot ears.

detail.diagnosis: A vet diagnoses heat stress mainly from the history and examination. They will want to know the weather, the housing, water supply, recent transport or handling, and how quickly signs started. They check the body temperature with a thermometer. A healthy rabbit is roughly 38.5–40 °C, and readings clearly above this, along with fast breathing and hot ears, point to overheating. The vet listens to the heart and lungs, checks the gums for dehydration and shock, and looks for other diseases that could make the rabbit less able to cope. There is no single lab test. Blood tests may be used in a clinic to check for organ damage. If rabbits die, a post-mortem can show congested (blood-filled) lungs and organs and help rule out infections such as pasteurellosis or viral haemorrhagic disease. To help the vet, write down when signs began, the temperature in the hutch if you have a thermometer, how many rabbits are affected and their ages, and whether they had water. Keep any dead rabbits cool and covered for examination.
firstSteps: Move the rabbit immediately, gently and calmly, into the coolest shaded place you have, such as a cool room, under a tree or on a shaded cement floor with moving air.

Wet the ears with cool water using a damp cloth or sponge, because the ears are the rabbit's radiator. You can also dampen the fur lightly. Do not plunge the rabbit into cold or ice water, as this can send it into shock.
Offer clean, cool drinking water in a shallow dish. If the rabbit cannot drink by itself, do not force water into its mouth, because it may choke or breathe it into the lungs.
Improve airflow with a fan, or by fanning gently by hand. A plastic bottle of frozen water wrapped in a cloth placed beside the rabbit can help, as long as the rabbit can move away from it.
Stop cooling once the rabbit is breathing more slowly, the ears feel only slightly warm and it starts to respond, so you do not chill it too much.

Call your vet or animal health officer straight away, especially if the rabbit is breathing with its mouth open, cannot stand or is having fits. Rabbits can seem to recover and then get worse hours later.
Check all the other rabbits at once. Give extra water, shade the hutches and reduce crowding, because if one rabbit is overheating others are likely close behind.
Write down what happened: time, weather, number affected and any deaths. Do not give any medicines or home remedies unless your vet tells you to.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment aims to cool the rabbit safely, replace lost fluids, support the organs and prevent complications. The vet will continue controlled cooling while checking the temperature so the rabbit is not overcooled. They often give fluids by injection under the skin or into a vein to treat dehydration and shock. Some clinics may give oxygen to rabbits struggling to breathe. Depending on the case, the vet may use anti-inflammatory pain relief, which they will choose carefully because of the risk to dehydrated kidneys. They may also use medicines that help the gut start moving again and supportive feeding, because gut stasis is a common problem after heat stroke. Antibiotics do not treat heat stress. A vet will only use them if there is a real secondary infection, and using them without need adds to antimicrobial resistance (germs becoming resistant to medicines). All treatment must be prescribed by a vet. If any drugs are used in meat rabbits, follow the withdrawal period (the waiting time before the meat is safe to eat) the vet gives you. Mildly affected rabbits often improve within hours. Severely affected rabbits may need close care for a day or more and can still die from organ damage despite good treatment.
prevention: Give every hutch good shade all day. Plant trees or creepers, put up shade net, or build under a grass-thatch or makuti roof. Avoid placing hutches where the afternoon sun hits them directly.

Insulate iron sheet roofs with a ceiling, a layer of grass thatch, or sacks on top, and leave a gap for hot air to escape. In very hot spells, wetting sacks on the roof or walls cools the house as the water evaporates.
Make sure there is plenty of airflow. Use wire-mesh sides, raise hutches off the ground, keep openings facing the breeze, and avoid closed wooden boxes or hutches pushed against hot walls.

Provide clean, cool water at all times and check it several times a day in hot weather. Rabbits drink much more in heat. Use more than one drinker or heavy clay pots that stay cool and do not tip over, and keep nipple drinkers in the shade so the water does not heat up.
Avoid overcrowding. Give each rabbit enough space, reduce numbers per cage in the hot season and separate growers early.
Feed concentrates in the cool early morning and evening when rabbits eat best, and offer fresh, clean, juicy greens that add water. Do not feed wilted or mouldy forage.

Do all handling, mating, weighing and transport in the early morning or late evening. Transport rabbits in ventilated, shaded crates, never in sacks or closed car boots, and never leave them parked in the sun.

Plan breeding so that late pregnancy and kindling (giving birth) avoid the hottest months where possible. Keep breeding bucks in the coolest part of the rabbitry, and keep nest boxes clean with only as much bedding as needed.
Keep rabbits at a healthy body condition, because fat rabbits overheat faster. Groom or clip long-haired breeds like Angora before the hot season.
Hang a simple thermometer in the rabbit house. When it rises towards 28–30 °C, start extra cooling such as wet sacks, more water and frozen water bottles in the cages.
detail.impact: Heat stress can wipe out profit on a rabbit farm quickly. A single hot afternoon can kill several rabbits, often the most valuable pregnant does, nursing does and heavy growers. Kits in nest boxes are especially likely to die. Rabbits that survive eat less, so growers take longer to reach market weight and feed is wasted. Does conceive less often, may lose pregnancies, produce less milk and give smaller litters. Bucks can become temporarily sterile, and fertility may take several weeks to return after the weather cools, which leaves gaps in the breeding calendar. Deaths during transport to market or to buyers are a common and costly loss in Kenya. For smallholders who rely on regular sales of meat rabbits or breeding stock, these losses can mean missed income for months.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on how hot the rabbit got, for how long, and how quickly it was cooled. Rabbits caught early, with fast breathing and red ears but still alert, usually recover well once moved to shade and given water. Rabbits breathing with an open mouth, unable to stand or having fits are in serious danger, and many die even with treatment. Survivors may have kidney, liver or gut problems in the following days, so watch their eating and droppings closely. Bucks may take several weeks to regain full fertility. Pregnant does that survive may still lose their litter. Good housing and water management prevent most cases, which makes heat stress one of the most preventable causes of rabbit death.

faqs.q: Can I dip my rabbit in a bucket of cold water to cool it quickly?
faqs.a: No. Putting a rabbit into cold or ice water can cause shock and can make it too cold, and wet fur dries slowly. Instead, wet the ears and lightly dampen the fur with cool water, put the rabbit in shade with moving air, and offer drinking water. Stop cooling once it is breathing more slowly and responding.

faqs.q: Why are my does not getting pregnant during the hot months?
faqs.a: Heat affects both sexes. Bucks exposed to high temperatures can become temporarily infertile, and this may last several weeks after the heat passes. Does under heat stress may not conceive, may lose pregnancies or may produce small litters. Keep bucks in the coolest part of the rabbitry, mate in the early morning or evening, and plan breeding around the hottest months where possible. If problems continue in cool weather, ask your vet to check for other causes.

faqs.q: Is it okay to keep rabbits under an iron sheet roof?
faqs.a: It can work, but bare iron sheets get very hot by midday and can push the temperature inside past what rabbits can tolerate. Add insulation such as a ceiling, a layer of grass thatch or sacks, leave space above the cages for hot air to escape, and keep the sides open with wire mesh. In very hot weather, wet sacks on the roof help cool the house.

faqs.q: Should I give antibiotics to a rabbit that collapsed in the heat?
faqs.a: No, not on your own. Heat stress is caused by high temperature, not germs, so antibiotics do not treat it. Using them without need wastes money and helps create resistant germs. The rabbit needs cooling, water and vet care. A vet may decide on other medicines such as fluids or pain relief, and will only use antibiotics if there is a real infection.

faqs.q: How can I keep rabbits cool if I have no electricity for fans?
faqs.a: Use shade from trees, shade net or thatch, and keep hutches raised with open mesh sides facing the breeze. Hang wet sacks on the roof or sides so evaporation cools the air. Freeze plastic bottles of water overnight if you or a neighbour has a fridge, or use clay pots of water, and place them in the cages for rabbits to lie against. Always give plenty of clean, cool water, and avoid handling rabbits in the afternoon.

faqs.q: My rabbits die when I take them to market. What am I doing wrong?
faqs.a: Transport is one of the most common causes of heat deaths. Rabbits packed in sacks, closed boxes or car boots, or left in the sun at a market or stage, overheat very quickly. Travel in the early morning, use ventilated crates with space for each rabbit, keep them shaded and out of direct sun, avoid long waits, and do not overcrowd.

heat-stress.imagePrompt: A white New Zealand rabbit lying stretched out flat on its side on the wire floor of a backyard hutch on a hot sunny day, with bright red ears, a damp chin and fast-moving flanks, under a bare iron sheet roof.
heat-stress.seoDescription: Heat stress in rabbits: spot fast breathing, red ears and wet chin early, give safe first aid, and keep your Kenyan rabbitry cool in the hot dry season.

card.headline: Long front teeth and wet chin
card.look: The front teeth stick out, curl or point sideways instead of meeting neatly. The rabbit drools, has a wet, matted chin and chest fur, picks at food then drops it, and slowly gets thinner.
card.action: Open the lips gently, look at the front teeth, weigh the rabbit, and book a vet visit now. Get help the same day if it has stopped eating.

aka: Molar spurs (sharp points on cheek teeth)
detail.summary: Malocclusion means the teeth do not meet and wear against each other properly. A rabbit's teeth grow all its life, so a tooth that is not worn down keeps getting longer. The long teeth cut the mouth, block eating and can push into the jaw and eye area. The rabbit can starve slowly, and a rabbit that stops eating can quickly develop deadly gut problems. Most cases come from too little hay or grass, or from inherited jaw shape, so most are preventable.
detail.cause: All of a rabbit's teeth are open-rooted. This means they keep growing for its whole life, the front teeth by a few millimetres every week. In a healthy rabbit, chewing on rough, fibrous food like grass and hay grinds the teeth down as fast as they grow. Malocclusion happens when this balance breaks. Some rabbits are born with a short upper jaw or a mis-shaped skull, so the front teeth never meet. This is common in dwarf and lop-eared breeds and is passed from parents to young. Other rabbits develop it later. The main cause is a soft diet of pellets, kitchen scraps or soft greens with too little hay. Pellets need only short, crushing bites, not the long side-to-side grinding that wears the cheek teeth. Damage can also start from injury, such as pulling on wire cage bars or a fall that breaks a tooth. Infection, or poor calcium and vitamin D supply affecting bone strength, may play a part, though experts still debate how much. Once the teeth are uneven, the problem builds on itself. The back cheek teeth (molars and premolars) grow sharp points called spurs. These cut the tongue and cheeks, so chewing hurts and the rabbit eats less hay, which makes wear even worse. The roots can also grow longer and push into the jawbone and toward the eye. There they can block the tear duct, which causes eye discharge, and they can lead to tooth-root abscesses, pockets of pus in the jaw.
spread: It is not contagious. It cannot pass from one rabbit to another by contact, so cage-mates will not catch it.
Inherited jaw shape passes from parents to kits, so breeding from an affected buck or doe spreads the problem through your herd.
A diet low in long fibre is the biggest trigger. Examples are mainly pellets, bread, kitchen leftovers, or soft greens like cabbage and sukuma wiki without enough hay or dry grass.
Chewing or pulling on wire mesh and cage bars can bend, crack or misalign the front teeth, especially in bored or crowded rabbits.
Injury from falls, rough handling or fights can break a tooth, so its partner tooth is no longer worn and overgrows.
Dry seasons, when good grass is scarce and farmers rely more on pellets or scraps, can raise the number of cases a few months later.
Rabbits kept indoors in dark sheds with no sunlight and a poor mineral balance may have weaker bone around the teeth, though this link is still uncertain.
detail.atRisk: Any rabbit can be affected. Some face more risk than others. Dwarf breeds, lop-eared breeds and other rabbits with short, flat faces are most likely to have the inherited form, which often shows in young rabbits from a few weeks to months old. Commercial breeds kept for meat in Kenya, such as New Zealand White, Californian, Chinchilla and Flemish Giant, more often get the acquired form. This happens when they are fed mostly pellets or kitchen waste in cages with little hay. Older rabbits and breeding does kept for several years are at higher risk, because uneven wear builds up over time. Rabbits in wire-mesh hutches with nothing safe to chew are more likely to damage their front teeth. Farms that keep breeding from the same few animals without checking their teeth can see the problem become common in a line.

early: Wet chin, neck or front legs, with damp or matted fur from drooling (often called 'slobbers').
Picking up food then dropping it, or chewing slowly or on one side only.
Choosing soft foods like pellets or soft leaves and leaving hay, grass stems and harder vegetables.
Front teeth that look too long, curve outward or sideways, or do not meet in a neat line when you lift the lips.
Small, fewer or misshapen droppings, because the rabbit is eating less fibre.
Less grooming, so the coat looks rough, and soiled fur around the tail.
Watery or slightly cloudy discharge from one or both eyes.
advanced: Clear weight loss: the spine and hip bones feel sharp under your hand.
Front teeth that curl into the lips, gums or up toward the nose and cause sores.
A firm or soft lump along the jaw or under the eye, which may be a tooth-root abscess.
Thick white or yellow eye discharge and a wet, crusted face, with one eye sometimes looking pushed forward.
Grinding teeth loudly, hunching in a corner, and not wanting to move, all signs of pain.
Bad smell from the mouth, or blood-tinged saliva.
Complete refusal of food with few or no droppings. This is an emergency, because the gut can stop working within about a day.

lookalikes.name: Snuffles (Pasteurella and other respiratory infections)
lookalikes.howToTell: Snuffles causes sneezing, a runny nose and matted fur on the inside of the front legs from wiping the nose. Eye discharge can occur in both. In snuffles the rabbit usually still chews normally and the teeth look fine. With dental disease the drooling and food dropping are the main signs. The two can also happen together.

lookalikes.name: Gut stasis (gastrointestinal stasis)
lookalikes.howToTell: Gut stasis is when the gut slows or stops. The rabbit stops eating, makes few or no droppings and may have a tight, painful belly, but there is usually no drooling or wet chin. It is often caused by dental pain, so a rabbit with stasis should always have its teeth checked.

lookalikes.name: Coccidiosis
lookalikes.howToTell: Coccidiosis is caused by a tiny gut or liver parasite. It mainly affects young weaners and causes weight loss, a pot belly and diarrhoea, often in several rabbits at once. Teeth and chin are normal. Dental disease usually affects single rabbits and causes drooling, not diarrhoea.

lookalikes.name: Heat stress
lookalikes.howToTell: A heat-stressed rabbit may drool slightly. But it also breathes fast, has hot, red ears, lies stretched out and appears on hot afternoons in tin-roofed hutches. It improves quickly when cooled. Dental drooling continues day after day whatever the weather.

detail.diagnosis: A vet starts by looking at the front teeth and feeling the jaw, face and under the eyes for lumps, heat or pain. The back teeth sit deep in a narrow mouth. The vet checks them with an otoscope (a small lighted viewer) or a mouth speculum, and a full check often needs sedation. X-rays of the skull, where available, show tooth roots, bone damage and abscesses, and help decide whether repeated trimming or removal is better. If there is pus, the vet may take a sample to find the right antibiotic. Before the visit, write down what the rabbit eats each day, when the drooling or food dropping started, and any change in droppings. If you can, weigh it on a kitchen or hanging scale and note the weight. Tell the vet whether its parents or littermates had similar teeth. Bring the rabbit in a secure, well-ventilated box with some hay so the vet can watch it try to eat.
firstSteps: Handle the rabbit calmly, wrapped in a towel. Gently lift the lips to look at the front teeth and check for sores, then feel along the jaw for lumps.
Weigh the rabbit and write down the weight, date, what it is eating and the number of droppings. This helps the vet see whether it is getting worse.
Offer plenty of fresh soft grass, soft leafy greens and hay, all chopped short, so it can keep eating while you wait. Never leave a rabbit without food.
Give clean water in a shallow bowl as well as any nipple bottle, because a sore mouth makes bottle drinking hard.
Keep the rabbit in a quiet, shaded, cool spot away from stress. Separate it only if cage-mates are stealing its food or bullying it.
Gently wipe and dry the wet chin and eye area with a clean damp cloth to prevent skin sores and flies.
Do not cut the teeth yourself with nail clippers, pliers or wire cutters. This often splits the tooth, exposes the painful centre and lets infection into the root.
If the rabbit has eaten nothing and made few or no droppings for about 12 hours or more, treat it as an emergency and get to a vet the same day.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on which teeth are affected and how badly. For overgrown front teeth, the vet usually shortens and reshapes them with a dental burr, a small high-speed grinding tool, which is safer than clippers. For spurs on the back teeth, the rabbit normally needs sedation or anaesthesia so the vet can file the sharp points smooth. Because the teeth keep growing, most rabbits need repeat trimming every few weeks to few months for life. If the front teeth will never meet properly, the vet may advise removing them under anaesthesia. Rabbits manage well without front teeth if food is cut into small pieces. Pain relief, commonly a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug such as meloxicam, helps the rabbit start eating again. A rabbit that has stopped eating may need syringe feeding with a soft fibre mash and medicines to restart the gut. Tooth-root abscesses are hard to treat. They may need surgery to clean or remove the bad tooth plus a longer antibiotic course. Antibiotics should only be used when there is infection, and only as prescribed, because misuse breeds resistant bacteria (antimicrobial resistance). Some antibiotics are dangerous to rabbits and can kill them by upsetting their gut, so never use leftover livestock drugs. If treated rabbits are meat animals, follow the vet's withdrawal period before slaughter. For commercial meat units where lifelong trimming is not practical, the vet may advise humane culling of badly affected animals. All medicines and doses must be prescribed by a vet.
prevention: Feed hay or dry grass as the main food, available all day, making up most of what the rabbit eats. Rhodes grass, Boma Rhodes or good mixed grass hay all work.
Use pellets as a measured supplement only, not the main diet. Too many pellets fill the rabbit without wearing its teeth.
Add fresh grass, weeds such as sow thistle (mchunga) and safe leafy browse, plus some vegetables, but do not rely on soft kitchen scraps, bread or ugali.
Store hay for the dry season after the long and short rains, so rabbits do not switch to a soft diet when grazing is poor.
Give safe things to chew, such as untreated branches from fruit trees or other non-toxic trees and hard grass stems. These reduce boredom and stop rabbits chewing cage wire.
Check the teeth of every rabbit every few weeks and at weaning, sale and before breeding. Gently lift the lips and look for neat, even front teeth.
Do not breed from rabbits with crooked teeth or a short jaw, or from parents that produced affected kits. Cull or keep them only as non-breeders.

Give a balanced mineral supply through a good-quality ration, and let rabbits have some daylight or sunlight where safe. Avoid extra vitamin D or calcium without vet advice, because too much can harm rabbits.
Handle rabbits carefully and keep hutches safe from falls to prevent broken teeth and jaw injuries.
detail.impact: On a Kenyan rabbit farm, dental disease costs money quietly. Affected rabbits eat less, grow slowly and reach market weight late or not at all. Does with sore mouths lose condition, produce less milk and raise smaller, weaker litters. Repeated vet trimming adds cost that a meat rabbit may not pay back. Abscesses and long-term eye infections can make a rabbit unsellable. Where poor genetics is the cause, the problem can spread through a breeding line and lower the value of breeding stock sold to other farmers. Deaths often come from gut stasis or starvation after a rabbit stops eating. The good news is that the main prevention, plenty of hay or grass, is cheap and also improves gut health and growth across the whole herd.
detail.outlook: The outlook depends on the cause and on how early it is caught. Rabbits whose problem comes from diet often do well if the teeth are corrected early and they are moved onto a high-hay diet. Some then need little further trimming. Rabbits born with a mis-shaped jaw usually need lifelong regular trimming or tooth removal. Many still live comfortably if the owner keeps up with care. The outlook is poorer once roots have grown into the jaw or eye area, or when tooth-root abscesses form. These often return and can shorten life. A rabbit that stops eating needs fast help, because gut stasis can kill even when the teeth themselves could have been fixed.

faqs.q: Can I just cut my rabbit's long front teeth with nail clippers?
faqs.a: It is not recommended. Clippers crush and split the tooth, which can leave sharp edges, expose the painful pulp inside and let infection reach the root. The tooth also grows back quickly, often even more crooked. A vet uses a dental burr to shorten and shape the tooth safely. If no burr is available, ask the vet what they advise for your area.

faqs.q: My rabbits eat plenty of pellets. Why are their teeth still overgrown?
faqs.a: Pellets are soft and broken up quickly, so rabbits eat them fast with little grinding. Rabbit teeth are designed to wear down on tough grass and hay, chewed with long side-to-side movements for many hours a day. Make hay or dry grass the main food and reduce pellets to a measured amount.

faqs.q: Why does my rabbit have eye discharge if the problem is in its teeth?
faqs.a: The roots of the upper cheek teeth and front teeth sit very close to the tear duct, the small tube that drains tears from the eye to the nose. When roots grow too long, they press on or block this duct. Tears then spill over the face and can become infected. Eye discharge together with drooling or food dropping strongly suggests dental disease.

faqs.q: Should I keep breeding from a doe with crooked teeth if she is a good mother?
faqs.a: It is better not to. If the crooked teeth are inherited, she can pass the problem to her kits and they to theirs. You may end up with many affected rabbits. Keep her as a non-breeder or cull her, and choose breeding stock with clean, even teeth.

faqs.q: Is it better to cull an affected meat rabbit or treat it?
faqs.a: This depends on the rabbit's value, how bad the problem is and what treatment costs in your area. A young meat rabbit with an inherited short jaw will need trimming for life, which is rarely worth it commercially. A valuable breeding animal with a diet-related problem may recover well. Discuss it with your vet. If you cull, do it humanely, and respect any medicine withdrawal period before eating the meat.

faqs.q: How often should I check my rabbits' teeth?
faqs.a: A quick look every few weeks during routine handling is a good habit. Also check at weaning, before sale and before mating. Weighing rabbits regularly also helps, because slow weight loss is often the first clue that a rabbit is struggling to eat.

overgrown-teeth.imagePrompt: Close-up photo of a white New Zealand rabbit in a wooden hutch with its lips gently parted to show long, curved, misaligned front teeth and a wet, matted chin, with hay in the background.
overgrown-teeth.seoDescription: Overgrown teeth in rabbits: spot drooling, wet chin, dropping food and weight loss early, what to do before the vet, and how good hay prevents it.

card.headline: Round crusty bald patches on face
card.look: Coin-shaped patches of hair loss with grey-white scales or yellowish crusts, usually around the eyes, nose, ears and front paws. The rabbit is often bright and eating, and may scratch only a little.
card.action: Put on gloves, move the affected rabbit to a separate cage, and ask a vet to confirm it before it spreads to other rabbits or your family.

aka: Choa (Swahili, for ringworm in people and animals)
detail.summary: Ringworm is a skin infection caused by a fungus, not a worm. In rabbits it causes round, scaly, hairless patches, mostly on the head, ears and feet. It is rarely fatal, but it spreads easily between rabbits and to people, especially children. The fungus survives for a long time in hutches and equipment, so one case can become a long-running problem on a rabbitry if it is not handled properly.
detail.cause: In rabbits, ringworm is mostly caused by a fungus called Trichophyton mentagrophytes. Less often, Microsporum canis, the type often carried by cats and dogs, is involved. These fungi are called dermatophytes, which means 'skin plants'. They feed on keratin, the tough protein that makes up hair, the outer layer of skin and claws. The fungus produces tiny seeds called spores. When spores land on skin that is slightly damaged, damp or belongs to a rabbit with weak defences, they grow into the hair shafts and the top layer of skin. The infected hairs become weak and break off close to the skin, leaving a bald patch. The skin reacts by producing scales and crusts. The infection spreads outwards in a ring, which is why the patches are often round and may look healthier in the middle. Some rabbits carry spores in their fur without showing any signs at all. These 'silent carriers' are a common reason why ringworm keeps coming back on a farm. If the rabbit scratches or the skin cracks, bacteria can enter and cause a secondary infection with pus, redness and pain.
spread: Direct contact between rabbits, for example when young rabbits share a cage, when does nurse kits, or during mating.
Spores left on hutches, cages, nest boxes, feeders, bedding, hay and wooden surfaces, where they can survive for many months, often longer than a year.
Shared equipment such as brushes, nail clippers, carrying baskets, gloves and sacks used to move rabbits to market.
People's hands and clothes, when a farmer handles an infected rabbit and then touches healthy ones without washing.
Newly bought rabbits, especially from markets or other farms, that may be silent carriers with no visible patches.
Cats, dogs and rodents around the rabbitry, which can carry ringworm fungi and bring them into the hutches.
Damp, overcrowded, poorly ventilated housing, which allows spores to build up and makes the skin easier to infect.
Stress from weaning, transport, poor feeding or another illness, which weakens the rabbit's natural defences and lets a carrier infection flare up.
detail.atRisk: Young rabbits, especially weanlings between about one and four months old, are most often affected because their immune systems are still developing and they are usually kept in groups. Does that are nursing, old rabbits and rabbits with other illnesses, poor nutrition or heavy mite burdens are also at higher risk. Any breed can get ringworm, including New Zealand White, California, Chinchilla and local crosses. Problems are more common in crowded rabbitries, in wooden hutches that are hard to disinfect, and in houses that are damp and poorly ventilated. In Kenya, cases often increase during the long and short rains when humidity is high and hutches stay damp. Farms that buy breeding stock frequently, use shared transport baskets, or let cats and dogs into the rabbit house face a higher risk of introducing the fungus.

early: One or a few small, round patches of thinning or missing fur, often around the eyes, the base or tips of the ears, the nose or the muzzle.
Fine grey or white flakes like dandruff on and around the patch, sometimes with broken, stubby hairs at the edges.
Slightly reddened or pinkish skin where the fur has fallen out.
Mild scratching or rubbing of the face with the front paws, though many rabbits are hardly itchy at all.
Fur that comes away easily when you gently touch the edge of the patch.
The rabbit usually stays bright, active and eating normally, which makes the problem easy to overlook.
advanced: Patches that grow larger and join together, covering much of the face, ears, neck or body.
Thick yellowish or grey crusts, sometimes raised and lumpy, over the bald areas.
Infection of the front paws and around the nails, with scaly, crusty skin and occasionally misshapen claws.
Moist, sore or pus-filled areas where bacteria have entered scratched skin, often with a bad smell.
More intense scratching and restlessness if the skin becomes infected or very inflamed.
Several rabbits in the same cage or row showing similar patches, and sometimes red, itchy ring-shaped rashes on the farmer or family members.
Poor growth and weight loss in young rabbits with widespread disease, usually when another illness or poor feeding is also present.

lookalikes.name: Ear mites (ear canker, Psoroptes cuniculi)
lookalikes.howToTell: Ear mites cause thick, brown-grey, flaky crusts packed inside the ear canal and ear flap, with strong head shaking, ear scratching and sometimes drooping ears. Ringworm patches are usually on the outside of the ear, the face and paws, and the rabbit shakes its head much less.

lookalikes.name: Fur mites (Cheyletiella, 'walking dandruff')
lookalikes.howToTell: Fur mites cause lots of dandruff and thin fur mainly along the back, between the shoulders and at the base of the tail. If you look closely in good light, some of the 'dandruff' may move. Ringworm patches are more clearly round and are usually on the head, ears and feet.

lookalikes.name: Mange (Sarcoptes or Notoedres mites)
lookalikes.howToTell: Mange is usually very itchy. The rabbit scratches constantly and develops thick crusts on the nose, lips, eyelids, ears and toes, often spreading quickly with thickened, cracked skin. Ringworm is usually only mildly itchy. Because both can affect the face and paws, a vet's skin scraping is the safest way to tell them apart.

lookalikes.name: Fur chewing (barbering) or rabbit syphilis (treponematosis)
lookalikes.howToTell: With barbering, rabbits chew each other's fur, leaving short, cut hair over normal-looking skin with no scales or crusts, often on the back or flanks. Rabbit syphilis causes crusty sores mainly on the nose, lips, eyelids and genital area, and is passed on during mating. Ringworm causes scaly, round, bald patches with broken hairs, and the genitals are usually not the main site.

detail.diagnosis: A vet will first examine the rabbit closely, looking at the shape and position of the patches and checking the ears, back and feet to rule out mites. They may use a special ultraviolet torch called a Wood's lamp. Some Microsporum infections glow green under this light, but the more common Trichophyton type usually does not glow, so a negative result does not rule ringworm out. The vet may pluck a few hairs and scrape a little scale from the edge of the patch to look at under a microscope for fungal spores. The most reliable test is a fungal culture, where hairs and scales are placed on a special growth medium in a laboratory. This can take one to three weeks to give a result. Some laboratories can also run faster DNA-based tests. A skin scraping for mites is often done at the same time because mites and ringworm can occur together. Before the vet arrives, write down when you first saw the patches, how many rabbits are affected, their ages, any new rabbits bought recently, whether cats or dogs visit the rabbit house, and whether anyone in the family has an itchy skin rash. Do not wash, clip or apply anything to the patches before the visit, because this can make the tests less accurate.
firstSteps: Wear gloves, or at least wash your hands well with soap and water, every time you handle an affected rabbit, and handle healthy rabbits first and sick ones last.
Move the affected rabbit, and any rabbits sharing its cage, to a separate cage away from the main rabbitry, ideally one that is easy to clean such as a wire cage.
Check every rabbit on the farm carefully in good light, looking at the face, ears, paws and back, and note which ones have patches.
Remove and burn or bury soiled bedding, loose fur and hay from the affected cage, and keep the cage as dry and well ventilated as possible.
Stop selling, buying or lending rabbits, especially breeding stock, until a vet has checked the herd, so you do not spread the fungus to other farms.
Keep a separate brush, gloves and feeding container for the isolated rabbits, and do not share clippers or transport baskets.
Keep children away from the affected rabbits, and if anyone in the family develops a red, itchy, ring-shaped rash, take them to a health facility.

Avoid home remedies such as used engine oil, paraffin, strong disinfectants or crushed tablets on the skin, as these can burn the skin, poison the rabbit and delay proper treatment, then call your vet or County veterinary office for advice.
detail.vetTreatment: Treatment depends on how many rabbits are affected and how severe the patches are, and it must be prescribed by a vet. For a few small patches, the vet may recommend topical treatment, meaning medicine applied to the skin, such as antifungal creams, shampoos or rinses containing drugs like miconazole or enilconazole. Fur around the patches may be gently clipped to help the medicine reach the skin, with the clippings safely destroyed. For widespread disease or a whole group of rabbits, the vet may prescribe an antifungal medicine given by mouth, such as griseofulvin or itraconazole. Griseofulvin can harm unborn kits, so it must never be used in pregnant does or breeding bucks unless the vet decides otherwise. Treatment usually lasts several weeks and should continue until the vet confirms the rabbit is clear, often with a repeat culture, because patches can look healed while spores are still present. Antibiotics do not kill ringworm fungus. They are only useful if a bacterial infection has developed in scratched or broken skin, and should be used only when a vet prescribes them, at the full course given, to reduce the risk of antimicrobial resistance. Many antifungal medicines are not approved for meat animals, so if you keep rabbits for meat, ask your vet about the withdrawal period, which is the time you must wait after treatment before slaughtering for food, and do not sell or eat treated rabbits before it has passed. The vet will also advise on cleaning the environment, because treating the rabbit without cleaning the hutch often leads to reinfection. Expect new hair to start growing back within a few weeks of effective treatment, although full recovery of a heavily affected herd can take one to three months.
prevention: Quarantine every new rabbit for at least three to four weeks in a separate cage, checking the face, ears and paws regularly, before mixing it with your herd.
Buy breeding stock from known, reputable breeders and inspect rabbits closely in good light before paying, rejecting any with scaly or bald patches.
Avoid overcrowding, especially of weaners, and give each rabbit enough space so that skin-to-skin contact and stress are reduced.
Keep the rabbit house dry and well ventilated, with a sound roof, raised hutches and good drainage, paying extra attention during the long and short rains.

Clean cages regularly, removing droppings, fur and old bedding, and disinfect them between batches with a product your vet or agrovet confirms is effective against fungal spores, such as a diluted household bleach solution on surfaces that can tolerate it.
Use wire or smooth, easy-to-clean materials where possible, since old, cracked wooden hutches hold spores and are very hard to disinfect.
Do not share brushes, clippers, gloves, sacks or carrying baskets between rabbits or farms without cleaning them first.
Feed a balanced diet of good-quality pellets or a well-planned mix of fresh forage, hay and clean water, and control mites and other illnesses, so rabbits have strong natural defences.
Keep cats, dogs and rodents out of the rabbit house as much as possible, since they can carry ringworm fungi.
detail.impact: Ringworm rarely kills rabbits, but it costs Kenyan rabbit farmers money in several ways. Rabbits with visible patches are hard to sell, especially as breeding stock, and buyers at markets or other farms may refuse them or pay much less. A farm that becomes known for skin problems can lose its reputation as a source of breeding animals. Young rabbits with heavy infections may grow more slowly, delaying the time they reach sale weight. Pelts from affected rabbits are damaged and of little value. Treatment takes time and money, because medicines, vet visits, laboratory tests and thorough cleaning of hutches all add up, and treated meat rabbits may need to be held back during the withdrawal period. Because the spores survive for a long time, a poorly controlled outbreak can keep returning batch after batch. There is also the cost and discomfort of family members or workers catching ringworm.
detail.humanHealth: Ringworm is a zoonosis, which means it can pass from animals to people. Children, the elderly and people with weak immune systems are most likely to be infected. In people it usually shows as a red, itchy, slightly raised ring-shaped rash, often on the hands, arms, neck or face, and sometimes as scaly bald patches on a child's scalp. To protect yourself, wear gloves when handling affected rabbits or cleaning their cages, wash your hands well with soap and water afterwards, and change and wash clothes after working in the rabbitry. Do not let children cuddle or play with rabbits that have patches. Keep affected rabbits out of the house. If anyone develops a suspicious rash, visit a health facility and mention that your rabbits have ringworm, as human ringworm is treated with medicines prescribed by a health worker. If meat rabbits are treated, observe the withdrawal period your vet gives so that drug residues do not reach people who eat the meat.
detail.outlook: The outlook is good for most rabbits. Ringworm is uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening, and some mild cases in healthy adult rabbits clear up on their own over weeks to a few months. With vet-guided treatment, most rabbits regrow their fur within a few weeks to a couple of months. Recovery is slower and less certain in very young rabbits, in rabbits with other illnesses or poor nutrition, and when bacterial infection has set in. The biggest reason for failure is reinfection from a contaminated hutch or from silent carriers in the herd. Farms that combine treatment with thorough cleaning, less crowding, dry housing and quarantine of new stock usually bring the problem under control.

faqs.q: Is ringworm really caused by a worm?
faqs.a: No. Despite the name, ringworm is caused by a fungus, a tiny mould-like organism that lives on skin and hair. The name comes from the round, ring-like shape of the patches. Dewormers will not help, so do not waste money on them for this problem.

faqs.q: Can I catch ringworm from my rabbits?
faqs.a: Yes. Ringworm spreads easily from rabbits to people, especially children. It usually causes a red, itchy ring-shaped rash on the skin. Wear gloves when handling affected rabbits, wash your hands with soap afterwards, and keep children away from them. If someone in the family develops a rash, take them to a health facility for treatment.

faqs.q: Will the patches go away without treatment?
faqs.a: Some mild cases in strong, healthy adult rabbits do heal on their own over several weeks or months. However, during that time the rabbit keeps shedding spores that infect other rabbits, the hutch and people. Young rabbits and heavily affected ones may get worse. It is better to have a vet confirm the problem and advise on treatment and cleaning so the whole herd is protected.

faqs.q: Can I eat or sell a rabbit that has ringworm?
faqs.a: Ringworm affects the skin, not the meat, but affected rabbits should not be sold live because they will spread the infection to other farms. If your rabbit has been treated with antifungal medicine, you must wait until the withdrawal period given by your vet has passed before slaughtering it for food. Handle the carcass with gloves and dispose of the skin and fur safely, as they carry spores.

faqs.q: How do I clean a hutch after ringworm?
faqs.a: First remove all bedding, droppings, fur and leftover feed and burn or bury them. Scrub the hutch with soap and water to remove dirt, because disinfectants do not work well on dirty surfaces. Then apply a disinfectant that works against fungal spores, such as a diluted bleach solution or a product your vet or agrovet recommends, and leave it to dry fully in the sun if possible. Repeat cleaning regularly during treatment. Old, cracked wooden hutches are very hard to clean and may need repair or replacement.

faqs.q: Why does ringworm keep coming back on my farm?
faqs.a: The usual reasons are spores left in hutches and on equipment, rabbits that carry the fungus without showing signs, and conditions that weaken the rabbits, such as damp housing, overcrowding and poor feeding. New rabbits bought without quarantine, and cats or dogs visiting the rabbit house, can also bring it back. Treating all in-contact rabbits as your vet advises, cleaning thoroughly and improving housing usually breaks the cycle.
